title: Part 2, Chapter 26
paragraphs: In which the comical adventure of the puppet showman continues, along with other things that are genuinely worth the telling

All fell silent, Tyrians and Trojans alike — by which I mean that everyone watching the show was hanging on the lips of the boy who explained its marvels — when drums and trumpets were heard sounding inside it and artillery going off. The noise quickly died away, and then the boy raised his voice and said, “This true history presented here before your worships is taken word for word from the French chronicles and from the Spanish ballads that are on everyone’s lips, even the lips of the boys in the streets. It tells how Señor Don Gaiferos rescued his wife Melisendra, who was held captive in Spain by the Moors in the city of Sansueña — for that was the name then given to what is now called Saragossa. And there you may see Don Gaiferos playing at the gaming tables, just as the song goes—
At the tables Don Gaiferos sits at play, For Melisendra is forgotten now.

And that figure you see there, with a crown on his head and a scepter in his hand, is the Emperor Charlemagne, said to be Melisendra’s father, who, furious at his son-in-law’s idleness and indifference, comes in to scold him. Notice how vehemently and forcefully he rebukes him — you would swear he was about to land half a dozen raps on him with that scepter; and in fact there are authors who say he did land them, and solid ones too. And after telling him at length how he was putting his honor at risk by failing to win his wife’s release, he said, as the tale has it,
I’ve said enough — now see to it.

Notice, too, how the emperor turns his back and leaves Don Gaiferos seething; and now watch how, in a burst of rage, he hurls the table and the gaming board away from him and calls urgently for his armor, and asks his cousin Don Roland to lend him his sword, Durindana; and how Don Roland refuses to lend it, offering instead to join him in the difficult enterprise he is undertaking. But the valiant, angry Gaiferos will not accept the offer, declaring that he alone is enough to rescue his wife, even if she were locked away in the deepest center of the earth; and with that he goes off to arm himself and start his journey at once. Now turn your eyes, your worships, to that tower appearing over there, which is meant to be one of the towers of the alcazar of Saragossa, known today as the Aljaferia; and that lady appearing on the balcony, dressed in Moorish fashion, is the peerless Melisendra, who many a time would gaze from there toward the road to France, consoling herself in her captivity with thoughts of Paris and her husband. Now watch a fresh incident, the like of which has perhaps never been seen before. Do you not see that Moor who, silently and stealthily, finger to his lips, creeps up on Melisendra from behind? See how he plants a kiss right on her lips, and how quickly she spits and wipes them with the white sleeve of her smock, and how she laments and tears her lovely hair, as if it were to blame for the offense. Notice also that stately Moor standing in that corridor: he is King Marsilio of Sansueña, who, having witnessed the Moor’s insolence, immediately orders him — even though the man is his kinsman and a great favorite — to be seized and given two hundred lashes while being paraded through the streets of the city in the customary way, with criers walking ahead of him and officers of justice behind. And here you see them coming out to carry out the sentence, although the crime has barely been committed; for among the Moors there are no indictments or remands as there are with us.”

At this point Don Quixote called out, “Child, child, get on with your story in a straight line and don’t go wandering into curves and tangents, for to establish a fact beyond doubt takes a great deal of proof and corroboration.” And from inside Master Pedro said, “Boy, stick to your text and do as the gentleman tells you; that’s the soundest course. Keep to your plainsong and don’t attempt counterpoint, for fancy harmonies have a way of breaking down from being too refined.”

“I will,” said the boy, and he continued, “This figure you see here on horseback, wrapped in a Gascon cloak, is Don Gaiferos himself. His wife, now avenged for the insolence of the lovesick Moor, has taken her place on the balcony of the tower with a calmer, more settled expression, and has caught sight of him without recognizing him; and taking her husband for some passing traveler, she speaks to him and holds with him the whole conversation and exchange of the ballad that runs—
If you, sir knight, are bound for France, Oh! ask there for Gaiferos—

—which I will not repeat here, since long-windedness breeds boredom. It is enough to see how Don Gaiferos reveals who he is, and how Melisendra’s joyful gestures show us that she has recognized him; and what is more, we now see her lowering herself from the balcony to seat herself on the haunches of her good husband’s horse. But ah, unlucky lady! the hem of her petticoat has snagged on one of the balcony’s bars, and she is left hanging in midair, unable to reach the ground. But see how merciful heaven sends help in our worst moments of need: Don Gaiferos rides up and, without caring whether the rich petticoat tears or not, takes hold of her and hauls her down to the ground by force; then with a single heave he sets her on his horse’s haunches, astride like a man, and tells her to hold on tight and wrap her arms around his neck, crossing them over his chest so she will not fall, since the lady Melisendra was not accustomed to riding that way. See, too, how the horse’s neighing shows how pleased he is with the gallant and beautiful burden he carries in his lord and lady. See how they wheel about and leave the city behind, and how joyfully and gladly they take the road to Paris. Go in peace, O peerless pair of true lovers! May you arrive safely in the homeland you long for, and may fortune set no obstacle in the way of your happy journey; may the eyes of your friends and kinsmen see you living out the rest of your days in peace and quiet — and may those days be as many as Nestor’s!”
Here Master Pedro called out again: “Simplicity, boy! None of your flights of fancy — all affectation is bad.”

The interpreter made no reply but went on: “There was no shortage of idle eyes — the kind that see everything — to watch Melisendra climb down and mount up, and word was carried to King Marsilio, who at once ordered the alarm to be sounded; and see what an uproar there is, and how the city is drowned in the sound of the bells pealing from the towers of all the mosques.”

“No, no,” said Don Quixote at this point; “on the matter of the bells Master Pedro is badly mistaken, for the Moors do not use bells, only kettledrums and a kind of small trumpet rather like our clarion; ringing bells like this in Sansueña is without question a great absurdity.”

Hearing this, Master Pedro stopped the ringing and said, “Don’t fuss over trifles, Señor Don Quixote, or demand a level of perfection that is beyond reach. Aren’t a thousand plays performed all around us almost every day, stuffed with thousands of errors and absurdities, and yet they run successfully and are received not only with applause but with admiration and everything else besides? Carry on, boy, and pay no attention; as long as I fill my purse, I don’t care if I show as many blunders as there are motes in a sunbeam.”

“Fair enough,” said Don Quixote; and the boy went on: “See what a numerous and glittering troop of horsemen rides out of the city in pursuit of the two faithful lovers — what a blaring of trumpets, what a sounding of horns, what a beating of drums and tabors! I fear they will overtake them and drag them back tied to the tail of their own horse, which would be a dreadful sight.”

Don Quixote, however, seeing such a swarm of Moors and hearing such a racket, decided it would be right to help the fugitives; and rising to his feet he cried out in a loud voice, “Never, as long as I live, will I allow foul play to be done in my presence against so famous a knight and so fearless a lover as Don Gaiferos. Halt, low-born rabble! Do not follow or pursue him, or you will have me to fight!” And matching deed to word, he drew his sword, leapt in a single bound right up to the show, and with unheard-of speed and fury began raining blows down on the puppet troop of Moors, toppling some, beheading others, crippling this one and smashing that one; and among many other strokes he delivered one downward cut which, if Master Pedro had not ducked, made himself small, and scrambled out of the way, would have sliced his head off as easily as if it had been made of marzipan. Master Pedro kept shouting, “Stop, Señor Don Quixote, stop! Can’t you see that these things you’re knocking down, killing, and destroying aren’t real Moors but only little pasteboard figures? Look — sinner that I am! — you’re wrecking and ruining everything I own!” But for all that, Don Quixote never stopped delivering a continuous shower of cuts, slashes, downstrokes, and backstrokes, and in the end, in less time than it takes to say two credos, he brought the whole show crashing to the ground, with all its fittings and figures hacked and broken to pieces, King Marsilio gravely wounded, and the Emperor Charlemagne split in two, crown and head together. The entire audience was thrown into an uproar; the ape fled to the roof of the inn; the cousin took fright; and even Sancho Panza himself was mightily afraid, for — as he swore once the storm had passed — he had never seen his master in such a furious rage.

With the show thus completely demolished, Don Quixote calmed down somewhat and said, “I wish I had standing before me right now all those who do not believe, or will not believe, how useful knights-errant are in the world. Just consider: if I had not been present here, what would have become of the brave Don Gaiferos and the fair Melisendra? You may be certain those dogs would have caught up with them by now and done them some outrage. When all is said, then — long live knight-errantry, above everything alive on earth today!”
“Let it live and welcome,” said Master Pedro at this, in a feeble voice, “and let me die, for my luck is so bad that I can say with King Don Rodrigo—
Yesterday I was lord of Spain; today I have not a single turret left that I can call my own.

Not half an hour ago — no, barely a minute — I saw myself master of kings and emperors, my stables full of countless horses and my trunks and sacks crammed with fine costumes beyond numbering; and now I find myself ruined and brought low, destitute and a beggar, and worst of all without my ape, for by my faith my teeth will have to sweat before I get him caught again. And all because of the reckless fury of this sir knight here, who is said to shelter orphans, right wrongs, and do other works of charity — yet in my case alone his generous intentions came up short, blessed and praised be highest heaven! Truly he must be the Knight of the Rueful Figure, to have so disfigured mine.”

Sancho Panza was moved by Master Pedro’s words and said to him, “Don’t weep and carry on so, Master Pedro; you’re breaking my heart. Let me tell you that my master, Don Quixote, is so catholic and scrupulous a Christian that if he comes to see he has done you any wrong, he will admit it and be glad to pay for it and make it good — with something extra on top.”

“If Señor Don Quixote would only pay me for some part of the work he has destroyed,” said Master Pedro, “I would be satisfied, and his worship would set his conscience at rest; for no one can be saved who keeps what belongs to another against the owner’s will and makes no restitution.”
“That is true,” said Don Quixote; “but so far, Master Pedro, I am not aware of having anything of yours.”

“What!” Master Pedro shot back. “And these relics lying here on the bare hard ground — what scattered and shattered them but the invincible strength of that mighty arm? And whose were the bodies they belonged to but mine? And how did I earn my living except by them?”

“Now I am fully convinced,” said Don Quixote, “of something I have believed many times before: that the enchanters who persecute me do nothing but set figures like these before my eyes and then change and transform them into whatever they please. In all truth and earnest, gentlemen, I assure you who hear me now that everything that took place here seemed to me to be taking place literally — that Melisendra was Melisendra, Don Gaiferos Don Gaiferos, Marsilio Marsilio, and Charlemagne Charlemagne. That is why my anger was stirred; and to be true to my calling as a knight-errant I sought to give aid and protection to the fleeing pair, and with that good intention I did what you saw. If it has turned out the opposite of what I intended, the fault is not mine but that of the wicked beings who persecute me. Even so, I am willing to sentence myself to pay the costs of this mistake of mine, though it did not spring from malice: let Master Pedro say what he wants for the ruined figures, and I will pay it on the spot in good, current money of Castile.”

Master Pedro bowed to him and said, “I expected nothing less from the rare Christian spirit of the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, true helper and protector of all destitute and needy wanderers. Let master landlord here and the great Sancho Panza act as arbitrators and appraisers between your worship and me of what these battered figures are worth, or might be worth.”

The landlord and Sancho agreed, and Master Pedro then picked up from the floor King Marsilio of Saragossa, minus his head, and said, “You can see for yourselves how impossible it is to restore this king to his former condition; so I think — subject to your better judgment — that for his death, decease, and demise I should be given four reals and a half.”
“Go on,” said Don Quixote.
“Well then, for this split from top to bottom,” Master Pedro continued, picking up the cloven Emperor Charlemagne, “it would not be asking much if I claimed five reals and a quarter.”
“That’s not a small sum,” said Sancho.
“Nor is it a large one,” said the landlord; “split the difference and call it five reals even.”

“Give him the whole five and a quarter,” said Don Quixote, “for the grand total of this notable disaster doesn’t turn on a quarter more or less. And finish up quickly, Master Pedro, for it’s getting on toward suppertime and I’m feeling certain stirrings of hunger.”
“For this figure,” said Master Pedro, “which has lost its nose and is missing an eye, and which is the fair Melisendra, I ask — and I’m being reasonable in my price — two reals and twelve maravedis.”

“The devil himself must be in it,” said Don Quixote, “if Melisendra and her husband aren’t at least at the French border by now, for the horse they rode looked to me to be flying rather than galloping. So don’t try to sell me a cat for a hare by showing me a noseless Melisendra here, when she may well be taking her ease with her husband in France at this very moment. God help each man to his own, Master Pedro, and let us all deal plainly and honestly; and now carry on.”

Master Pedro, seeing that Don Quixote was beginning to wander and slip back into his old delusion, had no intention of letting him get away, so he said, “Then this cannot be Melisendra; it must be one of the maids who waited on her. So if I’m given sixty maravedis for her, I’ll consider myself content and well paid.”

And so he went on, setting prices on a great many more smashed figures, which, after the two arbitrators had adjusted them to the satisfaction of both parties, came to forty reals and three-quarters; and on top of that sum, which Sancho paid out at once, Master Pedro asked for two reals more for the trouble of catching the ape.

“Give them to him, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “not for catching the ape but for getting drunk; and I would give two hundred this very minute, as a reward for good news, to anyone who could tell me for certain that the lady Doña Melisandra and Señor Don Gaiferos are now in France among their own people.”

“No one could tell us that better than my ape,” said Master Pedro, “though there’s no devil who could catch him now. Still, I suspect affection and hunger will drive him to come looking for me tonight; but tomorrow will soon be here, and then we shall see.”

In short, the storm over the puppet show blew over, and everyone supped in peace and good fellowship at the expense of Don Quixote, whose generosity knew no limits. Before daylight the man with the lances and halberds took his leave, and shortly after daybreak the cousin and the page came to say goodbye to Don Quixote — the one heading home, the other continuing his journey, toward which Don Quixote gave him twelve reals to help him along. Master Pedro had no wish to get tangled in any further exchanges with Don Quixote, whom he knew all too well; so he rose before the sun, gathered up the remains of his show, caught his ape, and went off to seek his own adventures. The landlord, who did not know Don Quixote, was as astonished by his mad antics as by his generosity. To conclude, Sancho, on his master’s orders, paid him very generously, and after taking their leave of him they left the inn at about eight in the morning and took to the road, where we shall leave them to travel on; for this is necessary to make room for the telling of certain other matters that are needed to clear up this famous history.

title: Part 2, Chapter 27
paragraphs: Which reveals who Master Pedro and his ape really were, and recounts the misfortune Don Quixote met with in the braying adventure, which did not end as he wished or as he had expected

Cide Hamete, the chronicler of this great history, opens this chapter with the words, “I swear as a Catholic Christian;” concerning which his translator observes that since Cide Hamete was a Moor—as he undoubtedly was—his swearing as a Catholic Christian could only mean this: that just as a Catholic Christian, when he takes an oath, swears, or ought to swear, to what is true, and speaks the truth in whatever he declares, so he too was telling the truth, as faithfully as if he had sworn as a Catholic Christian, in everything he chose to write about Don Quixote—above all in revealing who Master Pedro was, and what lay behind the fortune-telling ape that amazed every village with its divinations. He says, then, that anyone who has read the First Part of this history will remember perfectly well the Gines de Pasamonte whom Don Quixote set free, along with the other galley slaves, in the Sierra Morena—a kindness for which that malicious, ill-natured crew later gave him poor thanks and worse repayment. This Gines de Pasamonte—Don Ginesillo de Parapilla, as Don Quixote called him—was the one who stole Dapple from Sancho Panza; and because, through the printers' fault, neither the how nor the when of it appeared in the First Part, the matter has puzzled a good many readers, who blame the author's bad memory for what was really an error of the press. The truth is that Gines stole the ass while Sancho Panza slept on his back, using the same trick and contrivance that Brunello employed when he stole Sacripante's horse out from between his legs at the siege of Albracca; and, as has already been related, Sancho got him back afterwards. Now this Gines, fearing capture by the officers of the law, who were hunting him so as to punish him for his countless villainies and crimes—which were so many and so serious that he himself wrote a thick book recounting them—decided to move into the kingdom of Aragon, cover his left eye, and set up as a puppet-showman; for at this trade, as at sleight of hand, he was a consummate master. From some freed Christians returning out of Barbary he chanced to buy the ape, which he trained to climb onto his shoulder at a certain signal and to whisper in his ear, or seem to. Equipped in this way, before he entered any village with his show and his ape, he would find out in the nearest town, or from the likeliest informant he could get hold of, exactly what had happened there and to whom; and keeping it all firmly in memory, the first thing he did was put on his show—now one story, now another, but all of them lively, entertaining, and familiar. The moment the performance ended he would bring out his ape's talents, assuring the audience that the animal could divine everything past and present, though as for the future it had no power at all. For each question answered he charged two reals, and for some he gave a discount, according to how he judged his customers' pulse; and now and then, when he came to houses where he happened to know what had befallen the inhabitants, even if they asked no question rather than pay for one, he would give the ape its signal and then announce that it had told him such and such—which matched the facts exactly. By this means he won an extraordinary reputation, and everyone flocked after him; at other times, being very cunning, he framed his answers so that they fitted the questions; and since nobody pressed him or demanded to know how his ape did its divining, he made fools of them all and kept his purse full. The moment he stepped into the inn he recognized Don Quixote and Sancho, and with that knowledge it was easy to astound them and everyone else present; but it would have cost him dearly if Don Quixote had brought his hand down a little lower when he struck off King Marsilio's head and wiped out his whole cavalry, as recounted in the previous chapter.

So much for Master Pedro and his ape; and now back to Don Quixote of La Mancha. After leaving the inn he resolved to see, before anything else, the banks of the Ebro and the country round about, and only then enter the city of Saragossa, since the long interval remaining before the jousts gave him time enough for everything. With this plan in mind he took the road and travelled along it for two days without meeting any adventure worth setting down in writing, until on the third day, while climbing a hill, he heard a tremendous din of drums, trumpets, and musket fire. At first he supposed a regiment of soldiers must be passing that way, and to get a look at them he put spurs to Rocinante and rode up the hill. From the top he saw at its foot what looked to him like more than two hundred men, armed with weapons of every description—lances, crossbows, partisans, halberds, and pikes, along with a few muskets and a great number of bucklers. He rode down the slope and drew near enough to the company to see the flags plainly, make out their colours, and read the emblems they carried—above all one on a standard or ensign of white satin, on which was painted, with great realism, an ass like a small Sardinian donkey, head raised, mouth open, tongue out, in the very act and posture of braying; and around it, in large letters, ran these two lines—

They did not bray in vain,
our two alcaldes twain.

From this emblem Don Quixote concluded that these people must come from the braying town, and he said as much to Sancho, explaining to him what was written on the standard. He added that the man who had first told them the story had got it wrong in saying the two brayers were regidors, since by the verses on the standard they were alcaldes. To this Sancho answered, “Señor, there's no need to fuss over that, for it may well be that the regidors who brayed back then became alcaldes of their town afterwards, so they can carry both titles; and anyway it makes no difference to the truth of the story whether the brayers were alcaldes or regidors, so long as they really did bray—for an alcalde is every bit as likely to bray as a regidor.” In short, they saw clearly that the town that had been mocked had marched out to fight some other town that had jeered at it beyond what was fair or neighbourly.

Don Quixote rode forward to join them, much to Sancho's discomfort, for he never had any taste for getting mixed up in ventures of that kind. The men of the company took him into their midst, assuming he was someone on their side. Don Quixote, raising his visor, rode with an easy, confident air up to the standard with the ass on it, and all the leading men of the army gathered round to look at him, staring with the same astonishment everyone felt on seeing him for the first time. Don Quixote, noticing how intently they studied him, and that no one spoke to him or asked him anything, decided to make use of their silence; so, breaking his own, he raised his voice and said, “Good sirs, I beg you as earnestly as I can not to interrupt an argument I wish to lay before you, unless you find it offensive or tiresome; and should that happen, at the slightest sign from you I will set a seal on my lips and a gag on my tongue.”
They all told him to say whatever he pleased, for they would hear him out gladly.

With that permission Don Quixote continued, “I, sirs, am a knight-errant, whose calling is arms and whose profession is to protect those who need protection and to aid those in distress. Some days ago I learned of your misfortune and of the cause that drives you to take up arms again and again to avenge yourselves on your enemies; and having turned your case over many times in my mind, I find that, by the laws of combat, you are mistaken in considering yourselves insulted, for a private individual cannot insult an entire community—unless he defies it collectively as traitorous, because he cannot tell which particular person committed the treason for which he issues the challenge. We have an example of this in Don Diego Ordoñez de Lara, who defied the whole town of Zamora because he did not know that Vellido Dolfos alone had committed the treachery of killing his king; he therefore defied them all, and the vengeance and the answer concerned them all—though it is true that Señor Don Diego went rather too far, indeed well past the limits of a proper challenge, since he had no business defying the dead, or the waters, or the fishes, or those not yet born, and all the rest of it as the record sets out; but let that pass, for when anger boils over, the tongue has no father, no governor, and no bridle to restrain it. Since, then, no single person can insult a kingdom, a province, a city, a state, or a whole community, it is plain there is no cause to march out and avenge the defiance implied by such an insult, because it is no insult at all. A fine thing it would be if the people of the clock town came to blows every minute with everyone who called them by that name—or the Cazoleros, the Berengeneros, the Ballenatos, the Jaboneros, or the bearers of all the other names and nicknames that are forever in the mouths of boys and common folk! It would be a pretty state of affairs if all these illustrious cities took offence and exacted revenge and went about endlessly playing their swords like trombones over every petty squabble! No, no—God forbid! There are four causes for which sensible men and well-governed states ought to take up arms, draw their swords, and hazard their persons, lives, and fortunes. The first is to defend the Catholic faith; the second, to defend one's life, which accords with natural and divine law; the third, to defend one's honour, family, and property; the fourth, to serve one's king in a just war; and if we care to add a fifth—which can be counted under the second—it is the defence of one's country. To these five capital causes, as we may call them, others might be added that are just and reasonable and make taking up arms a duty; but to take them up over trifles, over things fit for laughter and amusement rather than offence, suggests that whoever does so is wholly lacking in common sense. What is more, to take an unjust revenge—and no revenge can be just—runs directly against the sacred law we profess, which commands us to do good to our enemies and to love those who hate us; a command that seems hard to obey only to those who have less of God in them than of the world, and more of the flesh than of the spirit. For Jesus Christ, true God and true man, who never lied and could not and cannot lie, said, as our lawgiver, that his yoke was easy and his burden light; and so he would never have laid on us any command impossible to keep. Thus, sirs, by both human and divine law, you are bound to keep the peace.”
“The devil take me,” Sancho said to himself at this, “if this master of mine isn't a theologian; or if he's not, then by my faith he's as like one as one egg is like another.”

Don Quixote paused to catch his breath, and, seeing that the silence still held, was inclined to carry on with his speech, and would have done so had Sancho not cut in with his usual quickness; for seeing his master stop, he seized his chance and said, “My lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, who was once called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance and is now called the Knight of the Lions, is a gentleman of great good sense who knows Latin and his own tongue like a university bachelor, and in everything he handles or advises on he proceeds like a seasoned soldier, with all the laws and rules of what they call combat at his fingertips; so there is nothing for you to do but let yourselves be guided by what he says, and let it be on my head if he is wrong. Besides, you have already been told it is foolishness to take offence at merely hearing a bray. I remember that when I was a boy I brayed whenever I felt like it, with no one to stop me, and so elegantly and naturally that when I brayed every ass in the town brayed back; yet I was none the less for that the son of my parents, who were highly respected people; and though more than one of the town's great and mighty envied me the gift, I didn't care two farthings about it. And so you can see I'm telling the truth, wait a moment and listen, for this art is like swimming—once learnt, it is never forgotten;” and then, gripping his nose, he began to bray with such force that all the surrounding valleys rang with the sound.

But one of the men standing near him, convinced he was mocking them, raised a long staff he carried in his hand and dealt him such a blow with it that Sancho dropped senseless to the ground. Don Quixote, seeing him so brutally treated, went lance in hand at the man who had struck him, but so many threw themselves between them that taking revenge was impossible. Far from it: finding a hail of stones pouring down on him, and crossbows and muskets beyond counting aimed his way, he wheeled Rocinante round and fled from their midst at the fastest gallop the horse could manage, commending himself to God with all his heart to bring him out of this danger, dreading at every stride that some ball would enter at his back and come out at his chest, and drawing breath every moment to check whether it had failed him yet. The men of the company, however, were content to watch him run, and did not fire on him. Sancho, barely come back to his senses, they set on his ass and sent off after his master—not that he was in any condition to steer the beast, but Dapple followed in Rocinante's tracks, unable to bear being parted from him for an instant. When Don Quixote had got some distance away he looked back, and seeing Sancho coming, waited for him, since no one was in pursuit. The men of the troop held their ground until nightfall, and as the enemy never came out to give battle, they marched back to their town in triumph; and had they known the ancient custom of the Greeks, they would have raised a trophy on the spot.

title: Part 2, Chapter 28
paragraphs: Concerning matters that Benengeli says the reader will understand, if he reads them attentively

When a brave man runs, the treachery has been exposed, and wise men save themselves for a better occasion. Don Quixote proved the truth of this maxim: yielding before the fury of the villagers and the hostile designs of the angry company, he took to flight and, without sparing a thought for Sancho or the danger he was leaving him in, put what he judged to be a safe distance behind him. Sancho followed, slung across his donkey, as has already been described. By the time he caught up he had come back to his senses, and on reaching his master he let himself slide off Dapple at Rocinante’s feet, aching, bruised, and thoroughly beaten. Don Quixote dismounted to inspect his wounds, but finding him sound from head to toe, he said, with some anger, “A fine moment you picked to start braying, Sancho! Where did you learn that it is wise to speak of rope in the house of a man who has been hanged? What accompaniment could you expect to the music of braying except a tune of cudgels? Thank God, Sancho, that they only blessed you with a stick just now instead of marking the sign of the cross on you—_per signum crucis_—with a cutlass.”

“I’m in no condition to answer,” said Sancho, “because I feel as if I were talking through my shoulders. Let’s mount up and get away from here. I’ll give up braying, but I won’t give up saying that knights-errant run away and leave their good squires behind to be beaten like privet, or ground into flour, at the hands of their enemies.”

“A man who withdraws is not running away,” Don Quixote replied, “for you should know, Sancho, that courage which does not rest on a foundation of prudence is called recklessness, and the feats of a reckless man are credited to good luck rather than to bravery. So I admit that I withdrew, but I deny that I fled; and in doing so I followed the example of many valiant men who have saved themselves for better times. The histories are full of such cases, but since reciting them would do you no good and give me no pleasure, I will spare you them for now.”

By now Sancho was back in the saddle with Don Quixote’s help, and once the knight had mounted Rocinante they made their way at an easy pace toward the shelter of a grove visible about a quarter of a league off. Every so often Sancho let out deep sighs and mournful groans, and when Don Quixote asked what caused such sharp suffering, he answered that he was so sore from the base of his spine up to the nape of his neck that it was nearly driving him out of his mind.

“The cause of that soreness,” said Don Quixote, “is no doubt this: the staff they struck you with was a very long one, so it caught you all the way down the back, where all the parts that hurt are located; and if it had reached any further, you would hurt even more.”

“By God,” said Sancho, “your worship has lifted a great doubt from my mind and settled the question in elegant style! Body of me! Was the cause of my soreness such a mystery that I needed to be told I’m sore everywhere the staff landed? If it were my ankles that ached, there might be some point in divining why; but it takes no great divination to work out that I hurt where they beat me. Faith, master of mine, another man’s troubles hang by a hair; every day I see more and more clearly how little I have to hope for from keeping company with your worship. If you’ve let me be thrashed this time, then next time, and a hundred times after, we’ll be back to the blanket-tossings of the other day and all the other tricks—and if they’ve landed on my shoulders now, they’ll be thrown in my face later on. I’d do far better (if I weren’t an ignorant brute who will never come to any good as long as I live)—far better, I say—to go home to my wife and children and feed them and raise them on whatever God sees fit to give me, instead of trailing after your worship along roads that lead nowhere and paths that are no paths at all, with little to drink and less to eat. And then there’s the sleeping! Measure out seven feet of earth, brother squire, and if that’s not enough for you, take as many feet again, for it’s all yours to arrange and you can stretch out to your heart’s content. I wish I could see the first man who meddled with knight-errantry burned and turned to ashes—or at least the first man who agreed to be squire to such fools as all the knights-errant of former times must have been. About those of today I say nothing, since your worship is one of them and I respect them, and because I know your worship knows a point more than the devil himself in everything you say and think.”

“I’d lay you a good wager, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “that now that you’re talking away with no one to stop you, you don’t feel a single pain in your whole body. Talk on, my son; say whatever comes into your head or your mouth, for as long as it spares you pain, the irritation your impertinence causes me will be a pleasure. And if you’re so eager to go home to your wife and children, God forbid that I should stand in your way. You hold money of mine: calculate how long it has been since we left our village this third time, work out what you can and should earn each month, and pay yourself out of your own hand.”

“When I worked for Tom Carrasco, the father of the bachelor Samson Carrasco that your worship knows,” Sancho replied, “I earned two ducats a month besides my food. I can’t say what I might earn with your worship, though I do know that a knight-errant’s squire has a harder time of it than a man who works for a farmer; for after all, however hard we farmhands toil all day long, at the worst we get our olla for supper at night and sleep in a bed—something I haven’t done since I entered your worship’s service, apart from the short while we spent in Don Diego de Miranda’s house, the feast I had off the skimmings I took from Camacho’s pots, and what I ate, drank, and slept at Basilio’s. All the rest of the time I’ve slept on the hard ground under the open sky, exposed to what they call the inclemencies of heaven, keeping myself alive on scraps of cheese and crusts of bread, and drinking water from the brooks or the springs we come across on these byways we travel.”
“I grant you, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “that everything you say is true. How much, do you think, ought I to give you over and above what Tom Carrasco paid you?”

“In my opinion,” said Sancho, “if your worship were to add on two reals a month, I’d count myself well paid—that is, as far as the wages for my labor go. But to compensate me for your worship’s pledge and promise to give me the governorship of an island, it would only be fair to add six reals more, bringing the whole to thirty.”

“Very well,” said Don Quixote. “It is twenty-five days since we left our village, so reckon it up, Sancho, according to the wages you have set for yourself, see how much I owe you in proportion, and pay yourself, as I said before, out of your own hand.”

“Oh, body of me!” said Sancho, “your worship is badly out in that reckoning; for where the promise of the island is concerned, we have to count from the day your worship promised it to me right up to this present hour we’re standing in.”
“Well then, Sancho, how long is it since I promised it to you?” said Don Quixote.
“If I remember rightly,” said Sancho, “it must be more than twenty years, give or take three days.”

Don Quixote gave his forehead a great slap, burst into hearty laughter, and said, “Why, counting the Sierra Morena and the whole course of our expeditions, I have been on the road barely two months, and you tell me, Sancho, that it is twenty years since I promised you the island? I see it now: you want all the money of mine you are holding to be swallowed up in your wages. If that is so, and that is what pleases you, I give it to you here and now, once and for all, and much good may it do you; for as long as it rids me of so worthless a squire, I will gladly be left a pauper without a penny. But tell me, you corrupter of the squirely laws of knight-errantry, where have you ever seen or read that any knight-errant’s squire haggled with his lord—‘you must pay me so much a month for my service’? Plunge, you scoundrel, rogue, monster—for that is what I take you to be—plunge, I say, into the _mare magnum_ of their histories, and if you can find that any squire ever said or even thought what you have just said, you may nail it to my forehead and throw in four sound slaps across my face besides. Turn the rein—or rather the halter—of your Dapple and be off home, for you shall not take one single step further in my company. O bread thanklessly eaten! O promises wasted! O man more beast than human being! Now, when I was about to raise you so high that, in spite of your wife, people would call you ‘my lord,’ now you leave me? You go now, when I had a firm and settled intention of making you lord of the best island in the world? Well, as you yourself have said before now, honey is not for the mouth of the ass. An ass you are, an ass you will remain, and an ass you will be when your life runs its course; for I know your days will reach their end before you ever notice or admit that you are a beast.”

Sancho watched Don Quixote intently all through this scolding, and remorse stung him so sharply that tears rose to his eyes, and in a pitiful, breaking voice he said, “Master of mine, I confess that to be a complete ass I lack nothing but a tail; if your worship will just fasten one on me, I’ll consider it rightly placed, and I’ll serve you as an ass for all the days I have left to live. Forgive me, take pity on my foolishness, and remember that I know very little, and that if I talk too much, it comes more from weakness than from malice. But he who sins and mends commends himself to God.”

“I would have been surprised, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “if you had got through a speech without slipping in some scrap of a proverb. Well, well, I forgive you—on condition that you mend your ways and stop showing yourself so fond of your own profit; try instead to be cheerful and take heart, and encourage yourself to look forward to the fulfillment of my promises, which may be delayed, but are not on that account impossible.”

Sancho said he would do so, and would keep his spirits up as best he could. They then entered the grove, where Don Quixote settled himself at the foot of an elm and Sancho at the foot of a beech—for trees of that kind, and others like them, always have feet but never hands. Sancho spent the night in pain, since the evening damp made the blow from the staff ache all the more, while Don Quixote passed it in his never-failing meditations; even so, they both snatched a few winks of sleep, and at first light they continued their journey in search of the banks of the famous Ebro, where something befell them that will be told in the following chapter.

title: Part 2, Chapter 29
paragraphs: Of the famous adventure of the enchanted boat

Traveling by stages, some already described and some passed over, Don Quixote and Sancho arrived at the river Ebro two days after leaving the grove, and the sight of it gave Don Quixote great delight as he studied and admired the beauty of its banks, the clearness of its stream, the gentleness of its current, and the abundance of its crystal waters; and the pleasant view awakened a thousand tender thoughts in his mind. Above all he kept returning to what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos, for although Master Pedro’s ape had told him that part of those things was true and part false, he leaned more toward their truth than their falsehood — the exact opposite of Sancho, who considered every bit of it an outright lie.

As they went along in this way, then, they spotted a small boat without oars or any other tackle, lying at the water’s edge and tied to the trunk of a tree growing on the bank. Don Quixote looked all around, and seeing no one, dismounted from Rocinante at once, without further ceremony, and told Sancho to get down from Dapple and tie both animals securely to the trunk of a poplar or willow that stood there. Sancho asked him the reason for this sudden dismounting and tethering. Don Quixote answered, “You must understand, Sancho, that this boat is plainly — and without the possibility of any other explanation — calling and inviting me to step into it and sail off to bring aid to some knight or other person of rank who needs it and is doubtless in serious trouble; for this is how things go in the books of chivalry and with the enchanters who appear and speak in them. When a knight is caught in some difficulty from which only the hand of another knight can free him, even though the two may be separated by two or three thousand leagues or more, the enchanters either lift him up on a cloud or supply a boat for him to enter, and in less than the blink of an eye they carry him wherever they choose and wherever his help is required. So, Sancho, this boat has been placed here for exactly that purpose; this is as true as that it is now daylight, and before the day is out, tie Dapple and Rocinante together, and then let God’s hand guide us; for I would not hold back from going aboard even if barefooted friars begged me to.”

“Since that’s how it is,” said Sancho, “and your worship insists on giving in to these — I don’t know whether I’m allowed to call them absurdities — at every turn, there is nothing for it but to obey and bow my head, remembering the proverb, ‘Do as your master bids you, and sit down to table with him;’ but even so, for the sake of easing my conscience, I warn your worship that in my opinion this boat is no enchanted one, but belongs to some of the fishermen of this river, for they catch the best shad in the world here.”

As he said this, Sancho tied up the animals, leaving them to the care and protection of the enchanters with no small sorrow in his heart. Don Quixote told him not to be troubled about abandoning the creatures, “for he who would carry them over such longinquous roads and regions would also see to it that they were fed.”
“I don’t understand that logiquous,” said Sancho, “and I’ve never once heard the word in all the days of my life.”
“Longinquous,” replied Don Quixote, “means far away; and it is no wonder you don’t understand it, since you are not obliged to know Latin — unlike certain people who claim to know it and don’t.”
“Well, now they’re tied,” said Sancho. “What do we do next?”

“What next?” said Don Quixote. “Cross ourselves and weigh anchor — I mean, climb aboard and cut the moorings that hold the boat;” and the boat began to drift slowly away from the bank. But when Sancho found himself a couple of yards out into the river, he began to tremble and to give himself up for lost; and nothing distressed him more than hearing Dapple bray and watching Rocinante straining to break loose, and he said to his master, “Dapple is braying out of grief at our leaving him, and Rocinante is trying to get free so he can plunge in after us. O dearest friends, peace be with you, and may this madness that is carrying us away from you turn into sober sense and bring us back to you.” And with that he began weeping so bitterly that Don Quixote said to him, sharply and angrily, “What are you afraid of, you coward? What are you crying about, you heart of butter-paste? Who is chasing you, who is troubling you, you soul of a tame mouse? What do you lack, sitting unsatisfied in the very lap of abundance? Are you by any chance trudging barefoot over the Riphaean mountains, instead of being seated on a bench like an archduke on the tranquil current of this pleasant river, from which in a short while we shall come out onto the open sea? But surely we have already come out and traveled seven or eight hundred leagues; and if I had an astrolabe here to take the height of the pole, I could tell you exactly how many we have covered — though either I know little, or we have already crossed, or shall shortly cross, the equinoctial line that divides the two opposite poles at the midpoint.”
“And when we come to that line your worship is talking about,” said Sancho, “how far will we have traveled?”

“A very great distance,” said Don Quixote, “for of the three hundred and sixty degrees that this terraqueous globe contains, as computed by Ptolemy, the greatest cosmographer known, we shall have covered one half by the time we reach the line I mentioned.”
“By God,” said Sancho, “your worship has given me a fine authority for what you say — putrid Dolly somebody-or-other transmogrified, or whatever it is.”

Don Quixote laughed at the version Sancho had made of “computed” and of the name of the cosmographer Ptolemy, and he said, “You should know, Sancho, that among the Spaniards, and among all those who sail from Cadiz for the East Indies, one of the signs by which they tell that they have passed the equinoctial line I described to you is that the lice die on every person aboard the ship — not a single one survives, nor could one be found in the whole vessel even if its weight in gold were offered for it. So, Sancho, you may as well run your hand down your thigh, and if you come upon anything alive, our doubt will be settled; if not, then we have crossed.”

“I don’t believe a word of it,” said Sancho; “still, I’ll do as your worship orders, though I don’t see what need there is for trying these experiments, since I can see with my own eyes that we haven’t moved five yards from the bank, or drifted two yards from where the animals are standing — for there are Rocinante and Dapple in the very same spot where we left them; and taking a fixed point, as I’m doing right now, I swear by all that’s good that we are not stirring or moving even at the pace of an ant.”

“Make the test I told you of, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “and pay no attention to anything else, for you know nothing of colures, lines, parallels, zodiacs, ecliptics, poles, solstices, equinoxes, planets, signs, and bearings — the measures of which the celestial and terrestrial spheres are composed. If you were acquainted with all of these things, or even some part of them, you would see plainly how many parallels we have cut across, what signs we have seen, and what constellations we have left behind and are leaving behind now. But once more I tell you: feel about and hunt, for I am certain you are cleaner than a sheet of smooth white paper.”

Sancho felt about, and running his hand gently and carefully down to the hollow of his left knee, he looked up at his master and said, “Either the test is a false one, or we have not come anywhere near where your worship says — not within many leagues of it.”
“Why, how is that?” asked Don Quixote. “Have you come upon anything?”

“On something — and on somethings,” answered Sancho; and shaking his fingers, he washed his whole hand in the river, along which the boat was gliding quietly in midstream, moved by no hidden intelligence or invisible enchanter, but simply by the current, which just there ran smooth and gentle.

They now caught sight of some large water mills standing in the middle of the river, and the moment Don Quixote saw them he cried out, “Do you see, my friend? There stands the castle or fortress where some knight must be lying captive, or some ill-treated queen, or infanta, or princess, for whose rescue I have been brought here.”
“What devil of a city, fortress, or castle is your worship talking about, señor?” said Sancho. “Can’t you see that those are mills standing in the river to grind corn?”

“Be quiet, Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Though they look like mills, they are not; I have already told you that enchantments transform things and alter their natural shapes. I don’t mean that they actually change them from one form into another, but that they appear to do so, as experience showed in the transformation of Dulcinea, the sole refuge of my hopes.”

By now the boat, having reached the middle of the stream, began to move rather less slowly than before. The millers who worked the mills, seeing the boat coming down the river and about to be sucked into the rush of the wheels, ran out in haste — several of them, carrying long poles to stop it — and since they were all covered in meal, their faces and clothes dusted white with flour, they made a sinister sight. They raised loud shouts, crying, “You devils of men, where are you going? Are you out of your minds? Do you want to drown yourselves, or be smashed to pieces in these wheels?”

“Didn’t I tell you, Sancho,” said Don Quixote at this, “that we had come to the place where I must show what the strength of my arm can do? Look at the ruffians and villains coming out against me; look at the monsters that oppose me; look at the hideous faces sent to frighten us! Now you shall see, you scoundrels!” And standing up in the boat, he began loudly hurling threats at the millers, shouting, “Ill-natured and worse-advised rabble, set at liberty and restore to freedom the person you hold captive in this fortress or prison of yours, whether of high station or low, of whatever rank or quality, for I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, also called the Knight of the Lions, for whom, by the decree of heaven above, the happy ending of this adventure is reserved.” And as he said it he drew his sword and began slashing at the air in the direction of the millers, who, hearing but not understanding all this nonsense, set about trying to stop the boat, which was now entering the rushing channel of the wheels. Sancho dropped to his knees and devoutly begged heaven to deliver him from such imminent danger — which it did, through the energy and quickness of the millers, who pushed against the boat with their poles and stopped it, though not without capsizing it and pitching Don Quixote and Sancho into the water. It was lucky for Don Quixote that he could swim like a goose, although the weight of his armor dragged him twice to the bottom; and had it not been for the millers, who dove in and hauled them both out, it would have been the fall of Troy for the pair of them. Once they were landed — more drenched than thirsty — Sancho got down on his knees and, with hands clasped and eyes lifted to heaven, prayed a long and fervent prayer to God to deliver him forever after from the reckless schemes and undertakings of his master. At that point the fishermen who owned the boat, which the mill wheels had battered to pieces, came up, and seeing it smashed, they set about stripping Sancho and demanding payment for it from Don Quixote; but he, with perfect calm, as if nothing at all had happened to him, told the millers and fishermen that he would gladly pay for the boat, on the condition that they hand over to him, free and unharmed, the person or persons being held captive in that castle of theirs.
“What persons or what castle are you talking about, madman? Do you mean to carry off the people who come to grind their corn at these mills?”

“Enough,” said Don Quixote to himself. “To try to persuade this rabble by entreaty to do anything virtuous would be preaching in the desert. In this adventure two powerful enchanters must have come up against each other, and one thwarts what the other attempts: one provided the boat for me, and the other overturned me. God help us — this whole world is nothing but schemes and machinations working at cross purposes with one another. I can do no more.” And then, turning toward the mills, he said aloud, “Friends, whoever you may be who lie shut up in that prison, forgive me that, to my misfortune and yours, I cannot deliver you from your misery; this adventure is doubtless reserved and destined for some other knight.”

With that he came to terms with the fishermen and paid fifty reals for the boat — money Sancho handed over very much against his will, remarking, “A couple more boat ventures like this one and our whole fortune will have gone to the bottom.”

The fishermen and the millers stood staring in astonishment at these two figures, so unlike ordinary men in their appearance, and could not for the life of them work out what Don Quixote’s remarks and questions were driving at; concluding that the pair were madmen, they left them and went their ways — the millers to their mills and the fishermen to their huts. Don Quixote and Sancho returned to their beasts, and to their life as beasts of burden, and so ended the adventure of the enchanted boat.

title: Part 2, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Of Don Quixote's adventure with a beautiful huntress

Knight and squire returned to their animals dejected and in a thoroughly sour mood—Sancho especially, for anything that touched their store of money touched his very heart, and whenever any of it was taken from him he felt as though someone had plucked out the apples of his eyes. So, without a word passing between them, they mounted and rode away from the famous river, Don Quixote sunk in thoughts of his love, Sancho brooding over his hopes of advancement, which at that moment seemed to him very far from being realized. Fool though he was, he could see plainly enough that his master's actions were all, or nearly all, completely senseless, and he began looking for a chance to slip away from his service one day and go home, without offering any explanation or saying any goodbye. Fortune, however, arranged things in a manner very different from what he had in mind.

It happened that the next day, toward sunset, as he came out of a wood, Don Quixote looked across a green meadow and noticed some people at the far end of it; drawing nearer, he saw that it was a hawking party. Closer still, he made out among them a lady of graceful bearing, mounted on a snow-white palfrey or hackney fitted with green trappings and a silver-mounted side-saddle. The lady herself was dressed in green, so richly and magnificently that she seemed magnificence itself in human form. On her left hand she carried a hawk, which convinced Don Quixote that she must be some great lady and the mistress of the whole hunting party—as indeed she was. So he said to Sancho, “Run, Sancho, my son, and tell that lady on the palfrey with the hawk that I, the Knight of the Lions, kiss the hands of her exalted beauty, and that if her excellence grants me leave, I will come and kiss them in person and put myself at her service in whatever lies within my power and her highness may command. And watch how you speak, Sancho—take care not to wedge any of your proverbs into the message.”
“A fine one you've found to wedge any in!” said Sancho. “You can trust me with that! This isn't the first time in my life I've carried messages to high and exalted ladies.”
“Apart from the one you carried to the lady Dulcinea,” said Don Quixote, “I am not aware that you have carried any other, at least not in my service.”

“True enough,” replied Sancho; “but a good payer isn't troubled by his pledges, and in a house where there's plenty, supper is quickly on the table. What I mean is, there's no need to tell me anything or warn me about anything—I'm ready for whatever comes and know a little about everything.”
“I believe it, Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Go then, and good luck to you, and God speed you on your way.”

Sancho set off at full tilt, driving Dapple beyond his usual pace, and reached the spot where the beautiful huntress was waiting. Dismounting, he knelt before her and said, “Fair lady, that knight you see over there, the Knight of the Lions by name, is my master, and I am a squire of his—at home they call me Sancho Panza. This same Knight of the Lions, who until recently went by the name of the Knight of the Rueful Countenance, sends me to ask whether it might please your highness to grant him leave so that, with your permission, approval, and consent, he may come and carry out his desire, which is—as he says and I believe—to serve your exalted loftiness and beauty. And if you grant it, your ladyship will be doing something that redounds to your honor, and he will receive a most distinguished favor and happiness.”

“Truly, squire,” said the lady, “you have delivered your message with every formality such messages demand. Stand up—it is not fitting that the squire of so great a knight as he of the Rueful Countenance, of whom we have heard a great deal in these parts, should stay on his knees. Rise, my friend, and tell your master that he is welcome to the service of myself and of the duke my husband, at a country house we keep nearby.”

Sancho stood up, as charmed by the good lady's beauty as by her well-bred manner and her courtesy, but most of all by her saying that she had heard of his master, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance; if she did not call him Knight of the Lions, it was doubtless only because he had taken that name so recently. “Tell me, brother squire,” asked the duchess (whose actual title is not known), “this master of yours—is he not the one about whom a history has been published, called ‘The Ingenious Gentleman, Don Quixote of La Mancha,’ who has as the lady of his heart a certain Dulcinea del Toboso?”

“The very same, señora,” replied Sancho; “and that squire of his who appears, or ought to appear, in the said history under the name of Sancho Panza, is me—unless they swapped me in the cradle, I mean in the printing press.”
“All of this delights me,” said the duchess. “Go, brother Panza, and tell your master that he is welcome on my estate, and that nothing could happen to me that would give me greater pleasure.”

Sancho went back to his master overjoyed with this gratifying answer, and reported everything the great lady had said, praising to the skies, in his rustic way, her rare beauty, her graceful liveliness, and her courtesy. Don Quixote sat up smartly in his saddle, planted himself firmly in his stirrups, adjusted his visor, spurred Rocinante, and rode forward with an easy air to kiss the duchess's hands. She, meanwhile, had sent for the duke her husband and, while Don Quixote was approaching, told him the whole story of the message. Since both of them had read the First Part of this history and knew from it about Don Quixote's mad streak, they awaited him with the keenest delight and eagerness to make his acquaintance, intending to play along with his fancy and agree with everything he said, and, for as long as he stayed with them, to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies customary in the books of chivalry they had read—for they themselves were very fond of such books.

Don Quixote now rode up with his visor raised, and as he made to dismount, Sancho hurried over to hold his stirrup for him; but in climbing down from Dapple he had the bad luck to catch his foot in one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he could not work it loose, and he was left dangling there with his face and chest on the ground. Don Quixote, who was not accustomed to dismounting without someone holding his stirrup, and assuming that Sancho had already arrived to hold it, swung himself off with a lurch and dragged Rocinante's saddle down after him—it must have been badly girthed—so that saddle and rider both ended up on the ground, to his considerable embarrassment and with plenty of curses muttered through his teeth against the unfortunate Sancho, whose foot was still caught in its shackle. The duke ordered his huntsmen to go to the aid of knight and squire, and they lifted up Don Quixote, badly shaken by his fall; limping, he advanced as best he could to kneel before the noble pair. This the duke would on no account allow; instead, dismounting from his own horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote, saying, “I am sorry, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that your first experience on my land should have been as unlucky a one as we have just witnessed; but the carelessness of squires is often the cause of worse accidents.”

“What has befallen me in meeting you, mighty prince,” replied Don Quixote, “cannot be called unfortunate, even if my fall had carried me all the way to the bottom of the bottomless pit, for the glory of having seen you would have raised me up and rescued me from it. My squire—God's curse upon him—is better at loosening his tongue to talk nonsense than at tightening a saddle's girths to keep it steady. But however I find myself, fallen or upright, on foot or on horseback, I shall always be at your service and at that of my lady the duchess, your worthy consort, worthy queen of beauty and supreme princess of courtesy.”
“Gently, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha,” said the duke; “where my lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso is concerned, it is not right that other beauties should be praised.”

Sancho, who by now had freed himself from his entanglement, was standing close by, and before his master could answer he said, “There's no denying it, and it must be insisted on, that my lady Dulcinea del Toboso is very beautiful; but the hare leaps up where you least expect it, and I've heard it said that what we call nature is like a potter who makes vessels out of clay, and whoever can make one fine vessel can just as easily make two, or three, or a hundred. I say this because, by my faith, my lady the duchess is in no way behind my mistress the lady Dulcinea del Toboso.”

Don Quixote turned to the duchess and said, “Your highness may be sure that no knight-errant in this world ever had a more talkative or more amusing squire than mine, and he will prove the truth of what I say if your highness is pleased to accept my services for a few days.”

To which the duchess answered, “That worthy Sancho is amusing I consider a very good thing, because it is a sign that he is shrewd; for wit and liveliness, Señor Don Quixote, as you well know, do not settle in dull minds, and since good Sancho is witty and lively, I hereby pronounce him shrewd.”
“And talkative,” Don Quixote added.
“All the better,” said the duke, “for many amusing things cannot be said in few words. But so as not to waste time talking, come, great Knight of the Rueful Countenance—”
“Of the Lions, your highness should say,” said Sancho, “for there's no Rueful Countenance, nor any such figure, anymore.”

“He of the Lions, then,” the duke went on. “I say, let Sir Knight of the Lions come to a castle of mine close by, where he will be given the reception owed to so exalted a person, the kind the duchess and I are accustomed to offer all knights-errant who come our way.”

By this time Sancho had set and girthed Rocinante's saddle, and once Don Quixote was on his back and the duke had mounted a fine horse, they placed the duchess between them and set out for the castle. The duchess asked Sancho to ride at her side, for she took endless pleasure in listening to his shrewd remarks. Sancho needed no urging; he worked himself in between her and the duke, who counted it rare good fortune to be receiving such a knight-errant and such a homespun squire at their castle.

title: Part 2, Chapter 31
paragraphs: Which treats of many great matters

Sancho's satisfaction was supreme at finding himself, as it seemed, an established favourite with the duchess. He was looking forward to discovering in her castle what he had found in Don Diego's house and Basilio's: he had always been fond of good living, and always seized any chance of feasting himself the moment one presented itself. The history tells us, then, that before they reached the country house or castle, the duke rode on ahead and instructed all his servants on how they were to treat Don Quixote. So the instant Don Quixote came up to the castle gates with the duchess, two lackeys or equerries, dressed in what they call morning gowns of fine crimson satin reaching down to their feet, hurried out, caught Don Quixote in their arms before he had seen or heard them, and said to him, "Your highness should go and help my lady the duchess down from her horse."

Don Quixote obeyed, and a great exchange of compliments followed between the two of them over the matter; but in the end the duchess's determination won, and she refused to dismount from her palfrey except in the arms of the duke, saying she did not consider herself worthy to impose so unnecessary a burden on so great a knight. At length the duke came out to help her down, and as they entered a spacious courtyard two beautiful young women came forward and threw a large mantle of the finest scarlet cloth over Don Quixote's shoulders. At the same instant all the galleries of the courtyard were lined with the menservants and maidservants of the household, crying, "Welcome, flower and cream of knight-errantry!" while all or most of them flung little pellets filled with scented water over Don Quixote and the duke and duchess. Don Quixote was utterly astonished at all this, and this was the first time he truly felt and believed himself to be a knight-errant in reality and not merely in his imagination, now that he saw himself treated in the same way he had read of such knights being treated in days of old.

Sancho, abandoning Dapple, hung on to the duchess and entered the castle, but feeling a twinge of conscience at having left the donkey on his own, he approached a respectable duenna who had come out with the rest to receive the duchess, and in a low voice he said to her, "Señora Gonzalez, or whatever your grace may be called—"

"I am called Doña Rodriguez de Grijalba," replied the duenna. "What is it you want, brother?" To which Sancho answered, "I'd be grateful if you could do me the favour of going out to the castle gate, where you'll find a grey donkey of mine; please have them put him in the stable, or put him there yourself, because the poor little beast is easily frightened and can't bear being alone at all."

"If the master is as wise as the servant," said the duenna, "we've struck a fine bargain. Be off with you, brother, and bad luck to you and to whoever brought you here. Go look after your donkey yourself — we, the duennas of this house, are not used to that sort of work."

"Well now, honestly," Sancho returned, "I've heard my master, who is the very treasure-house of stories, tell the story of Lancelot when he came from Britain, and he said that ladies waited on Lancelot and duennas waited on his horse. As for my donkey, I wouldn't trade him for Señor Lancelot's horse."
"If you're a comedian, brother," said the duenna, "save your jokes for somewhere they'll pass for wit and be paid for; from me you'll get nothing but a fig."
"At any rate it'll be a very ripe one," said Sancho, "because you won't lose the trick in years by even a point."

"Son of a bitch," said the duenna, blazing with anger, "whether I'm old or not is something I'll settle with God, not with you, you garlic-stuffed scoundrel!" — and she said it so loudly that the duchess heard her, and turning round and seeing the duenna in such a state of agitation, with her eyes flashing, asked her who she was quarrelling with.

"With this fellow here," said the duenna, "who has gone out of his way to demand that I go and put a donkey of his that's at the castle gate into the stable, holding it up to me as an example that they did the same I don't know where — that some ladies waited on one Lancelot, and duennas on his horse; and to top it all off, he called me old."

"That," said the duchess, "I would have considered the gravest insult that could be offered me." And addressing Sancho, she said, "You should know, friend Sancho, that Doña Rodriguez is very youthful, and she wears that hood more for the sake of authority and custom than because of her years."

"May all the rest of my years be unlucky," said Sancho, "if that's how I meant it. I only spoke because I'm so fond of my donkey, and I thought I couldn't commend him to a kinder-hearted person than the lady Doña Rodriguez."
Don Quixote, who was listening, said to him, "Is this appropriate conversation for the place, Sancho?"

"Señor," replied Sancho, "everyone has to mention what concerns him wherever he happens to be. I thought of Dapple here, and I spoke of him here; if I had thought of him in the stable I would have spoken there."

At which the duke observed, "Sancho is quite right, and there's no reason at all to find fault with him. Dapple shall be fed to his heart's content, and Sancho can rest easy — he'll be treated just as well as Sancho himself."

While this conversation, amusing to everyone except Don Quixote, was going on, they climbed the staircase and ushered Don Quixote into a chamber hung with rich gold cloth and brocade. Six young women relieved him of his armour and waited on him like pages, all of them prepared and instructed by the duke and duchess on what they were to do and how they were to treat Don Quixote, so that he might see and believe they were treating him like a knight-errant. When his armour was removed, there stood Don Quixote in his tight-fitting breeches and chamois doublet — lean, lanky, and long, with cheeks that looked as if they were kissing each other inside his mouth. He was such a figure that if the damsels waiting on him had not taken care to stifle their laughter (one of the particular instructions their master and mistress had given them), they would have burst out laughing. They asked him to let himself be undressed so they could put a shirt on him, but he absolutely refused, saying that modesty became knights-errant as much as valour did. However, he said they could give the shirt to Sancho. He shut himself in with Sancho in a room where there was a sumptuous bed, undressed, and put on the shirt; and then, finding himself alone with Sancho, he said to him, "Tell me, you newly fledged buffoon and old fool, do you think it right to offend and insult a duenna as deserving of reverence and respect as that one back there? Was that a moment to be thinking of your Dapple? Are these noble people likely to let the beasts fare badly when they treat their owners in such elegant style? For God's sake, Sancho, restrain yourself, and don't expose the threadbare weave so they can see what coarse, boorish stuff you're made of. Remember, sinner that you are, that a master is the more esteemed the more respectable and well-bred his servants are; and one of the greatest advantages princes have over other men is that they have servants as good as themselves to wait on them. Don't you see — shortsighted creature that you are, and unlucky mortal that I am! — that if they perceive you to be a coarse clown or a dull blockhead, they'll suspect me of being some impostor or swindler? No, no, Sancho my friend, keep clear, oh keep clear of these stumbling-blocks! Whoever lets himself become a chatterbox and a clown sinks into wretched buffoonery the first time he trips. Bridle your tongue, weigh your words before they escape your mouth, and bear in mind that we are now in quarters from which, by God's help and the strength of my arm, we shall come out mightily advanced in fame and fortune."

Sancho earnestly promised him he would keep his mouth shut and bite off his tongue before uttering a single word that wasn't entirely to the purpose and well considered, and told him he could rest easy on that point — it would never come out through Sancho who they really were.

Don Quixote got dressed, put on his baldric with his sword, threw the scarlet mantle over his shoulders, placed on his head a green satin cap the damsels had given him, and thus arrayed walked out into the great hall, where he found the damsels lined up in double file, the same number on each side, all with the equipment for washing his hands, which they presented to him with elaborate bows and ceremonies. Then twelve pages came in, together with the seneschal, to lead him to dinner, as his hosts were already waiting for him. They placed him in their midst and with great pomp and ceremony escorted him into another room, where a sumptuous table had been laid with just four place settings. The duchess and the duke came to the doorway to receive him, and with them a grave ecclesiastic — one of those who manage noblemen's households; one of those who, not being born great themselves, never know how to teach those who are how to behave as such; one of those who would have the greatness of great folk measured by their own narrowness of mind; one of those who, when they try to introduce economy into the household they run, lead it into pettiness. One of this sort, I say, must have been the grave churchman who came out with the duke and duchess to receive Don Quixote.

A great many polite speeches were exchanged, and at last, taking Don Quixote between them, they went to sit down at the table. The duke pressed Don Quixote to take the head of the table, and though he refused, the duke's pleas were so urgent he had to accept it.

The ecclesiastic sat down opposite him, and the duke and duchess at the sides. All this time Sancho stood by, gaping with amazement at the honour he saw shown to his master by these illustrious persons. Observing all the ceremonious back-and-forth between the duke and Don Quixote over who would take the head of the table, he said, "If your worship will give me leave, I'll tell you a story of what happened in my village about this business of seats."

The moment Sancho said this, Don Quixote trembled, sure he was about to come out with something foolish. Sancho glanced at him and, guessing his thoughts, said, "Don't worry that I'll go astray, señor, or say anything that isn't to the point. I haven't forgotten the advice your worship gave me just now about talking much or little, well or badly."
"I don't remember any of it, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Say what you like, but say it quickly."
"Well then," said Sancho, "what I'm about to say is so true that my master Don Quixote, who is here present, will keep me from lying."
"Lie as much as you like for all I care, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "I'm not going to stop you, but think about what you're going to say."
"I've considered and reconsidered so much," said Sancho, "that the bell-ringer's in a safe berth — as will be seen by what follows."
"It would be a good idea," said Don Quixote, "if your highnesses would order them to throw this idiot out, because he'll spout a heap of nonsense."
"By the duke's life, Sancho is not to be taken away from me for a single moment," said the duchess. "I'm very fond of him, because I know he is very shrewd."

"May your holiness's days be shrewd ones too," said Sancho, "for the good opinion you have of my wit, though there's none in me. But the story I want to tell is this: there was an invitation given by a gentleman in my town, a very rich one, of good family — for he was one of the Alamos of Medina del Campo, married to Doña Mencia de Quiñones, the daughter of Don Alonso de Marañon, Knight of the Order of Santiago, who was drowned at the Herradura — the one there was that quarrel about years ago in our village, which my master Don Quixote was mixed up in, to the best of my recollection, the one in which Tomasillo the scapegrace, son of Balbastro the blacksmith, was wounded. Isn't all this true, master mine? On your life, say so, so these gentlefolk don't take me for some lying chatterbox."
"So far," said the ecclesiastic, "I take you to be more of a chatterbox than a liar; but I don't know what I'll take you for by the time you're done."

"You cite so many witnesses and proofs, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that I have no choice but to say you must be telling the truth. Get on with it, and cut the story short, because at this rate you won't reach the end for two days."

"He's not to cut it short," said the duchess. "On the contrary, to please me he is to tell it just as he knows it, even if he doesn't finish for six days; and if he took that long they would be the most pleasant days I ever spent."
"Well then, sirs, I say," Sancho went on, "that this same gentleman, whom I know as well as I know my own hands — it's not a bowshot from my house to his — invited a poor but respectable labourer—"
"Get on, brother," said the churchman; "at the rate you're going, your story won't end this side of the next world."

"I'll stop short of halfway, God willing," said Sancho.
