"And so I say, this labourer, coming to the house of the gentleman I mentioned, the one who had invited him — God rest his soul, he's dead now; and what's more they say he died the death of an angel, though I wasn't there, because just at that time I had gone off to reap at Tembleque—"
"On your life, my son," said the churchman, "hurry back from Tembleque, and finish your story without burying the gentleman, unless you want to make more funerals."
"Well then, it so happened," said Sancho, "that as the pair of them were about to sit down to table — and I can see them now plainer than ever—"

The duke and duchess were greatly entertained by the irritation the worthy churchman showed at the long-winded, halting way Sancho had of telling his story, while Don Quixote was burning with rage and vexation.

"So, as I was saying," Sancho continued, "as the pair of them were about to sit down to table — as I said — the labourer insisted that the gentleman take the head of the table, and the gentleman insisted that the labourer take it, because his orders had to be obeyed in his own house. But the labourer, who prided himself on his politeness and good breeding, would not on any account, until the gentleman, out of patience, put his hands on his shoulders and forced him down into the seat, saying, 'Sit down, you stupid lout, because wherever I sit will be the head for you.' And that's the story, and honestly, I don't think it's been brought up out of place here."

Don Quixote turned every colour, and on his sunburnt face it left him mottled like jasper. The duke and duchess suppressed their laughter so as not to humiliate Don Quixote completely, because they saw through Sancho's impertinence. To change the subject and keep Sancho from coming out with more absurdities, the duchess asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea, and whether he had sent her any gifts of giants or villains lately, because surely he must have defeated a good many.

To which Don Quixote replied, "Señora, my misfortunes, though they had a beginning, will never have an end. I have defeated giants and I have sent her ruffians and villains; but where are they to find her, if she is enchanted and turned into the most ill-favoured peasant wench imaginable?"

"I don't know about that," said Sancho Panza. "To me she looks like the fairest creature in the world; at any rate, in nimbleness and jumping she won't yield to an acrobat. By my faith, señora duchess, she can spring from the ground onto the back of a donkey like a cat."
"You've seen her enchanted, Sancho?" asked the duke.
"Seen her? Well!" said Sancho. "Why, who the devil was it but me that first thought up the enchantment business in the first place? She's as enchanted as my father is."

The ecclesiastic, hearing them talk of giants and villains and enchantments, began to suspect this must be the Don Quixote of La Mancha whose story the duke was always reading. He had often rebuked the duke for it, telling him it was foolish to read such foolery. And becoming convinced his suspicion was correct, he turned to the duke and said very angrily, "Señor, your excellency will have to account to God for what this good man does. This Don Quixote, or Don Simpleton, or whatever his name is, cannot, I imagine, be quite such a blockhead as your excellency makes him out to be, holding out encouragement to him to keep going with his lunacies and follies." Then turning to address Don Quixote, he said, "And you, numskull — who put it into your head that you're a knight-errant, that you defeat giants and capture villains? Go your way and good luck to you. Go home and bring up your children if you have any, look after your business, and stop wandering about the world, gaping and making a laughing-stock of yourself to everyone who knows you and everyone who doesn't. In heaven's name, where did you discover that there are or ever were knights-errant? Where are there giants in Spain or villains in La Mancha, or enchanted Dulcineas, or any of the other silly things they tell about you?"

Don Quixote listened attentively to the reverend gentleman's words, and as soon as he saw he had finished speaking, regardless of the presence of the duke and duchess, he sprang to his feet with an angry look and an agitated face, and said — but the reply deserves a chapter of its own.

title: Part 2, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About the reply Don Quixote gave his critic, with other incidents grave and droll

Don Quixote, then, having risen to his feet, trembling from head to foot like a man dosed with mercury, said in a hurried, agitated voice, "The place I am in, the presence I stand in, and the respect I have always had for the profession to which your worship belongs, hold and bind the hands of my just indignation. For these reasons, and because I know, as everyone knows, that a clergyman's weapon is the same as a woman's — the tongue — I will with mine engage in equal combat with your worship, from whom one might have expected good advice instead of foul abuse. Pious, well-meant reproof requires a different bearing and arguments of another sort; in any case, to have reproved me in public, and so roughly, oversteps the bounds of proper reproof — that comes better with gentleness than with rudeness. And it isn't fitting to call the sinner an outright blockhead and fool, without knowing anything about the sin being reproved. Come, tell me — for which of the stupidities you have observed in me do you condemn and abuse me, and order me home to look after my house and wife and children, without knowing whether I have any? Is nothing more needed than to wangle one's way into other people's houses to rule over the masters — and that, perhaps, after having been brought up in all the narrowness of some seminary, without ever having seen more of the world than may lie within twenty or thirty leagues around — to be fit to lay down the law rashly for chivalry, and pass judgment on knights-errant? Is it perhaps an idle occupation, or is the time ill-spent that is spent in roaming the world in quest, not of its pleasures, but of those arduous toils by which the good rise upwards to the abodes of everlasting life? If gentlemen, great lords, nobles, men of high birth, were to rate me a fool, I should take it as an irreparable insult; but I don't care a farthing if clerics who have never entered upon or trod the paths of chivalry should think me foolish. A knight I am, and a knight I will die, if it pleases the Most High. Some take the broad road of overweening ambition; others that of mean and servile flattery; others that of deceitful hypocrisy, and some that of true religion. But I, guided by my star, follow the narrow path of knight-errantry, and in pursuit of that calling I despise wealth, but not honour. I have redressed injuries, righted wrongs, punished insolences, defeated giants, and crushed monsters. I am in love, for no other reason than that knights-errant are required to be so; but though I am, I am no carnal-minded lover — I am one of the chaste, platonic sort. My intentions are always directed to worthy ends: to do good to all and evil to none. And if a man who means this, does this, and makes this his practice deserves to be called a fool, then it is for your highnesses to say, most excellent duke and duchess."

"Good, by God!" cried Sancho. "Say no more in your own defence, master mine, because there's nothing more in the world to be said, thought, or insisted on. And besides — when this gentleman denies, as he has, that there are or ever have been knights-errant in the world, is it any wonder if he knows nothing of what he's been talking about?"
"Are you, perhaps, brother," said the ecclesiastic, "that Sancho Panza they mention, the one to whom your master has promised an island?"

"Yes, I am," said Sancho, "and what's more, I'm one who deserves it as much as anyone. I'm one of the sort — 'Attach yourself to the good, and you'll be one of them,' and of those who 'Not with whom you're bred, but with whom you're fed,' and of those who 'Lean against a good tree, and good shade covers them.' I've leant on a good master, and I've been going about with him for months, and please God I'll turn out to be just like him; long life to him and long life to me, because he won't be short of empires to rule, or I of islands to govern."
"No, friend Sancho, certainly not," said the duke. "In the name of Señor Don Quixote, I confer on you the government of one — not a small one either — that I have at my disposal."
"Down on your knees, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and kiss the feet of his excellency for the favour he has granted you."

Sancho obeyed, and on seeing this the ecclesiastic stood up from the table completely out of temper, exclaiming, "By the gown I wear, I'm almost ready to say that your excellency is as big a fool as these sinners. No wonder they're mad, when people in their senses sanction their madness! I leave your excellency to them, because as long as they are in the house, I will stay in my own and spare myself the trouble of reproving what I cannot remedy." And without uttering another word or eating another bite, he stalked off, the entreaties of the duke and duchess being entirely useless to stop him — not that the duke said much to him, because he couldn't, on account of the laughter the man's uncalled-for anger provoked.

When he had stopped laughing, he said to Don Quixote, "You have replied on your own behalf so stoutly, Sir Knight of the Lions, that there's no need to seek further satisfaction for this, which, though it may look like an offence, is not so at all — because, as women can give no offence, no more can ecclesiastics, as you very well know."

"That is true," said Don Quixote, "and the reason is that he who is not liable to offence cannot give offence to anyone. Women, children, and ecclesiastics, since they cannot defend themselves, though they may receive offence cannot be insulted — because between the offence and the insult there is, as your excellency very well knows, this difference: the insult comes from someone capable of offering it, who does so, and maintains it; the offence may come from any quarter without carrying insult with it. To take an example: a man is standing unsuspectingly in the street, and ten others come up armed and beat him; he draws his sword and conducts himself like a man, but the number of his opponents makes it impossible for him to achieve his purpose and avenge himself; this man suffers an offence but not an insult. Another example will make the same thing plain: a man is standing with his back turned, another comes up and strikes him, and after striking him takes to flight without waiting an instant, and the first man pursues him but does not overtake him; the one who received the blow received an offence, but not an insult, because an insult must be maintained. If the man who struck him, even though he did so sneakingly and treacherously, had drawn his sword and stood and faced him, then the one who was struck would have received offence and insult at the same time — offence because he was struck treacherously, insult because the striker maintained what he had done, standing his ground without running away. And so, according to the laws of the accursed duel, I may have received offence, but not insult, since neither women nor children can maintain it, nor can they wound, nor have they any way of standing their ground — and it's just the same with those who belong to religion. These three sorts of persons are without arms offensive or defensive, and so, although by nature they are bound to defend themselves, they have no right to offend anybody. And although I said just now that I might have received offence, I now say certainly not, because he who cannot receive an insult can still less give one. For these reasons I ought not to feel, nor do I feel, aggrieved at what that good man said to me. I only wish he had stayed a little longer, so I might have shown him the mistake he makes in supposing and maintaining that there are not and never have been any knights-errant in the world; if Amadis or any of his countless descendants had heard him say as much, I am sure it would not have gone well with his worship."

"I'll take my oath of that," said Sancho. "They would have given him a slash that would have split him from top to toe like a pomegranate or a ripe melon; they were just the fellows to put up with jokes of that sort! By my faith, I'm certain if Reinaldos of Montalban had heard the little man's words, he'd have given him such a smack on the mouth that he wouldn't have spoken for the next three years. Let him tackle them, and he'll see how he gets out of their hands!"
The duchess, listening to Sancho, was ready to die laughing, and in her own mind she set him down as droller and madder than his master; and there were quite a few just then who shared that opinion.

Don Quixote finally calmed down, and dinner came to an end, and as the tablecloth was being cleared, four damsels came in: one with a silver basin, another with a jug also of silver, a third with two fine white towels over her shoulder, and the fourth with her arms bared to the elbows and in her white hands (white they certainly were) a round ball of Naples soap. The one with the basin approached, and with arch composure and impudence thrust it under Don Quixote's chin. Wondering at such a ceremony, he said never a word, supposing it was the custom of that country to wash beards instead of hands. So he stretched his out as far as he could, and at that instant the jug began to pour and the damsel with the soap rubbed his beard briskly, raising snowflakes — for the soap lather was no less white — not only over his beard but all over his face, even over the eyes of the submissive knight, so that he was forced to keep them shut. The duke and duchess, who had known nothing about this, waited to see how the strange washing would end. The barber-damsel, when she had him a hand's breadth deep in lather, pretended there was no more water, and told the one with the jug to go and fetch some, while Señor Don Quixote waited. She did so, and Don Quixote was left the strangest and most ridiculous figure imaginable. Everyone present — and there were quite a few — was watching him, and as they saw him there with half a yard of neck on display, uncommonly brown, his eyes shut, and his beard full of soap, it was a great wonder, and only by enormous self-discipline, that they were able to keep from laughing. The damsels, the engineers of the joke, kept their eyes down, not daring to look at their master and mistress; and as for the duke and duchess, laughter and anger struggled within them, and they didn't know what to do — whether to punish the audacity of the girls or to reward them for the amusement they had had from seeing Don Quixote in such a state.

At length the damsel with the jug returned and they finished washing Don Quixote, and the one carrying the towels very deliberately wiped him and dried him; and all four together, making him a profound bow and curtsy, were about to leave when the duke, lest Don Quixote see through the joke, called out to the one with the basin, saying, "Come and wash me, and make sure there's water enough." The girl, sharp-witted and quick, came and placed the basin for the duke just as she had for Don Quixote, and they soon had him well soaped and washed, and after wiping him dry they made their bow and withdrew. It came out afterwards that the duke had sworn that if they had not washed him as they had Don Quixote, he would have punished them for their impudence — which they cleverly atoned for by soaping him as well.

Sancho watched the washing ceremony very attentively and said to himself, "God bless me, if only it were the custom in this country to wash squires' beards too as well as knights'. Because by God and on my soul, I want it badly; and if they gave me a scrape of the razor besides, I'd take it as an even greater kindness."
"What are you saying to yourself, Sancho?" asked the duchess.

"I was saying, señora," he replied, "that in the courts of other princes, I've always heard that when the cloth is taken away, they give water for the hands, but not lye for the beard; and that shows it's good to live long so you can see a lot. To be sure they say too that whoever lives a long life must endure a lot of evil, though to endure a washing of that sort is pleasure rather than pain."
"Don't be uneasy, friend Sancho," said the duchess. "I'll see to it that my damsels wash you, and even put you in the tub if necessary."
"I'll settle for the beard," said Sancho, "at least for now; and as for the future, God has decided what will be."
"Attend to worthy Sancho's request, seneschal," said the duchess, "and do exactly what he wishes."

The seneschal replied that Señor Sancho would be obeyed in everything; and with that he went off to dinner and took Sancho along with him, while the duke and duchess and Don Quixote remained at the table discussing a great variety of things, all bearing on the calling of arms and knight-errantry.

The duchess begged Don Quixote, since he seemed to have a sharp memory, to describe and portray for her the beauty and features of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, because, judging by what rumour trumpeted abroad of her beauty, she felt sure Dulcinea must be the fairest creature in the world, indeed in all La Mancha.

Don Quixote sighed on hearing the duchess's request, and said, "If I could pluck out my heart and lay it on a plate on this table here before your highness's eyes, it would spare my tongue the pain of telling what can hardly be thought, for in it your excellency would see her portrayed in full. But why should I attempt to depict and describe in detail, feature by feature, the beauty of the peerless Dulcinea — a burden worthy of other shoulders than mine, an enterprise in which the brushes of Parrhasius, Timantes, and Apelles, and the chisel of Lysippus ought to be employed, to paint it in pictures and carve it in marble and bronze, and Ciceronian and Demosthenian eloquence to sound its praises?"
"What does Demosthenian mean, Señor Don Quixote?" said the duchess. "It's a word I never heard in all my life."
"Demosthenian eloquence," said Don Quixote, "means the eloquence of Demosthenes, as Ciceronian means that of Cicero, who were the two most eloquent orators in the world."

"True," said the duke; "you must have lost your wits to ask such a question. Nevertheless, Señor Don Quixote would greatly gratify us if he would depict her for us; never fear, even in an outline or sketch she'll be something to make the fairest envious."

"I would do so, certainly," said Don Quixote, "had she not been blurred to my mind's eye by the misfortune that fell upon her a short time ago — one of such a nature that I am more ready to weep over it than to describe it. Your highnesses must know that, going a few days back to kiss her hands and receive her blessing, approval, and permission for this third sally, I found her altogether a different being from the one I sought. I found her enchanted and changed from a princess into a peasant, from fair to foul, from an angel into a devil, from fragrant to foul-smelling, from refined to clownish, from a dignified lady into a leaping tomboy — in a word, from Dulcinea del Toboso into a coarse Sayago wench."

"God bless me!" cried the duke aloud at this. "Who can have done the world such an injury? Who can have robbed it of the beauty that gladdened it, of the grace and gaiety that charmed it, of the modesty that gave it lustre?"

"Who?" replied Don Quixote. "Who could it be but some malignant enchanter, one of the many who persecute me out of envy — that accursed race born into the world to obscure and bring to nothing the achievements of the good, and to glorify and exalt the deeds of the wicked? Enchanters have persecuted me, enchanters persecute me still, and enchanters will continue to persecute me until they have sunk me and my lofty chivalry in the deep abyss of oblivion; and they injure and wound me where they know I feel it most. Because to deprive a knight-errant of his lady is to deprive him of the eyes he sees with, of the sun that gives him light, of the food by which he lives. I've said it many times before, and I say it once more now: a knight-errant without a lady is like a tree without leaves, a building without a foundation, or a shadow without the body that casts it."

"There's no denying it," said the duchess. "But still, if we are to believe the history of Don Quixote that has come out here lately to general applause, it is to be inferred from it, if I'm not mistaken, that you never saw the lady Dulcinea, and that she is nothing in the world but an imaginary lady — one you yourself begot and gave birth to in your brain, and adorned with whatever charms and perfections you chose."

"There's a good deal to be said on that point," said Don Quixote. "God knows whether there is a Dulcinea in the world or not, or whether she is imaginary or not imaginary; these are matters whose proof must not be pushed to extreme lengths. I have not begotten nor given birth to my lady, though I see her as she has to be — a lady who contains in herself all the qualities that would make her famous throughout the world: beautiful without blemish, dignified without haughtiness, tender and yet modest, gracious from courtesy and courteous from good breeding, and finally, of exalted lineage, because beauty shines forth and excels with a higher degree of perfection in those of good blood than in the fair of low birth."

"That is true," said the duke. "But Señor Don Quixote will give me leave to say what I am compelled to say by the story of his exploits that I've read, from which one infers that, granting there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, or out of it, and that she is in the highest degree beautiful as you have described her to us, as for the loftiness of her lineage she is not on a par with the Orianas, Alastrajareas, Madasimas, or others of that sort, with whom, as you well know, the histories abound."

"To that I may reply," said Don Quixote, "that Dulcinea is the daughter of her own deeds, that virtues rectify blood, and that lowly virtue is more to be regarded and esteemed than exalted vice. Besides, Dulcinea has something in her that may raise her to be a crowned and sceptred queen — because the merit of a fair and virtuous woman is capable of performing greater miracles than that. And though not formally, she virtually has higher fortunes within herself."

"I declare, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that in everything you say, you proceed most cautiously and with the bridle in hand, as the saying goes. From now on I'll believe in her myself, and I'll see to it that everyone in my house believes — even my lord the duke if necessary — that there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, that she is alive today, that she is beautiful and nobly born and deserves to have such a knight as Señor Don Quixote in her service, which is the highest praise I have it in my power to give her, or that I can think of. But I can't help having a small doubt, and a certain grudge against Sancho Panza. The doubt is this: the aforesaid history declares that the said Sancho Panza, when he carried a letter on your worship's behalf to the said lady Dulcinea, found her sifting a sack of wheat; and what's more, it says it was red wheat — a thing which makes me doubt the loftiness of her lineage."

To this Don Quixote made answer, "Señora, your highness must know that everything, or almost everything, that happens to me transcends the ordinary limits of what happens to other knights-errant, whether it's directed by the inscrutable will of destiny, or by the malice of some jealous enchanter. Now it's an established fact that all or most famous knights-errant have some special gift — one is invulnerable to enchantment, another is made of such impenetrable flesh that he cannot be wounded, like the famous Roland, one of the twelve peers of France, of whom it's said he could not be wounded except in the sole of his left foot, and only with the point of a stout pin and no other sort of weapon. And so, when Bernardo del Carpio slew him at Roncesvalles, finding that he couldn't wound him with steel, he lifted him up from the ground in his arms and strangled him, calling to mind in good time the death Hercules inflicted on Antaeus, the fierce giant said to be the son of Terra. I would infer from what I've mentioned that perhaps I may have some gift of this kind — not that of being invulnerable, because experience has proved to me many times that I am of tender flesh and not at all impenetrable; nor that of being proof against enchantment, because I've already seen myself thrust into a cage in which all the world would not have been able to confine me except by force of enchantments. But since I delivered myself from that one, I'm inclined to believe there's no other that can harm me. And so, these enchanters, seeing they can't exert their vile craft against my person, take revenge on what I love most, and try to rob me of life by maltreating that of Dulcinea, in whom I live. And therefore I am convinced that when my squire carried my message to her, they changed her into a common peasant girl, engaged in such a mean occupation as sifting wheat; but as I have already said, that wheat was not red wheat, nor wheat at all, but grains of oriental pearl. And as a proof of all this, I must tell your highnesses that, coming to El Toboso a short time ago, I was altogether unable to find the palace of Dulcinea; and the next day, though Sancho my squire saw her in her own proper shape, which is the fairest in the world, to me she appeared to be a coarse, ill-favoured farm-girl, by no means well-spoken either — she who is propriety itself. And so, since I am not and, so far as one can judge, cannot be enchanted, it is she who is enchanted, blighted, altered, changed, transformed; in her my enemies have taken their revenge on me, and for her shall I live in ceaseless tears until I see her restored to her original state. I have mentioned this so that nobody should mind what Sancho said about Dulcinea's winnowing or sifting; for as they changed her to me, it's no wonder if they changed her to him. Dulcinea is illustrious and well-born, and of one of the noble families of El Toboso, which are many, ancient, and good. In which, most assuredly, the share of the peerless Dulcinea is no small one, through whom her town will be famous and celebrated in ages to come, as Troy was through Helen, and Spain through La Cava — though with a better title and tradition. For another thing: I would have your graces understand that Sancho Panza is one of the drollest squires that ever served a knight-errant. Sometimes there is a sharpness about his simplicity that it's an amusement to try and work out whether he is simple or sharp. He has mischievous tricks that stamp him a rogue, and blundering ways that prove him a fool. He doubts everything and believes everything; when I think he's about to come down headlong from sheer stupidity, he comes out with something so shrewd it sends him up to the skies. After all, I would not exchange him for another squire, even if I were given a city to boot, and that's why I am in doubt whether it will be a good idea to send him to the government your highness has bestowed on him. Although I perceive in him a certain aptitude for the work of governing — so that, with a little trimming of his understanding, he would manage any government as easily as the king does his taxes; and besides, we already have ample experience that it doesn't require much cleverness or much learning to be a governor, because there are a hundred around us who scarcely know how to read and yet govern like gerfalcons. The main point is that they should have good intentions and be desirous of doing right in all things, because they'll never lack for people to advise and direct them in what they have to do, like those knight-governors who, being no lawyers, pronounce sentences with the aid of an assessor. My advice to him will be to take no bribe and surrender no right, and I have some other little matters in reserve, which will come out in due season for Sancho's benefit and the advantage of the island he is to govern."

The duke, duchess, and Don Quixote had reached this point in their conversation when they heard voices and a great hubbub in the palace, and Sancho burst abruptly into the room, glowing with anger, with a straining-cloth tied around him by way of a bib, and followed by several servants — or more properly speaking, kitchen-boys and other underlings — one of whom carried a small trough full of water that from its colour and impurity was plainly dishwater. The one with the trough pursued him everywhere he went, trying with the utmost persistence to thrust it under his chin, while another kitchen-boy seemed bent on washing his beard.
"What is all this, brothers?" asked the duchess. "What is it? What do you want to do to this good man? Do you forget he is a governor-elect?"
To which the barber kitchen-boy replied, "The gentleman will not let himself be washed as is customary, and as my lord and the señor his master have been."

"Yes I will," said Sancho, in a great rage, "but I'd like it to be with cleaner towels, clearer lye, and not such dirty hands. There's not so much difference between me and my master that he should be washed with angels' water and I with devil's lye. The customs of countries and princes' palaces are only good as long as they cause no annoyance, but the way of washing they have here is worse than doing penance. I have a clean beard, and I don't need to be freshened up in that fashion, and whoever comes to wash me or touch a hair of my head — I mean to say my beard, with all due respect — I'll give him a punch that will leave my fist sunk in his skull. These ceremonies and soapings are more like jokes than the polite attentions of one's host."

The duchess was ready to die with laughter when she saw Sancho's rage and heard his words; but it was no pleasure to Don Quixote to see him in such a sorry state, with the dingy towel about him and the hangers-on of the kitchen all around him. So, making a low bow to the duke and duchess as if to ask their permission to speak, he addressed the rabble in a dignified tone: "Here now, gentlemen! Leave that young man alone, and go back where you came from, or anywhere else if you like. My squire is as clean as anyone, and those troughs are no more proper for him than narrow, thin-necked jars. Take my advice and leave him be, because neither he nor I understand joking."

Sancho took the word out of his mouth and went on, "No, let them come and try their jokes on the country bumpkin — it's about as likely I'll stand for it as that it's now midnight! Let them bring me a comb here, or whatever they please, and curry this beard of mine, and if they get anything out of it that offends against cleanliness, let them clip me to the skin."

At this the duchess, laughing all the while, said, "Sancho Panza is right, and always will be in everything he says. He is clean, and as he says himself, he doesn't need to be washed; and if our ways don't please him, he's free to choose. Besides, you promoters of cleanliness have been excessively careless and thoughtless — I don't know whether I shouldn't say audacious — to bring troughs and wooden utensils and kitchen dishcloths, instead of basins and jugs of pure gold and towels of Holland linen, to such a person and such a beard. But after all, you're ill-bred and ill-conditioned, and spiteful as you are, you can't help showing the grudge you bear the squires of knights-errant."

The impudent servants, and even the seneschal who came with them, took the duchess to be speaking in earnest, so they removed the straining-cloth from Sancho's neck, and with something like shame and confusion in their faces, they all went off and left him. Whereupon Sancho, seeing himself safe out of what to him had seemed the most extreme danger, ran and fell on his knees before the duchess, saying, "From great ladies, great favours may be looked for. The favour your grace has done me today cannot be repaid with anything less than wishing I were dubbed a knight-errant, to devote myself all the days of my life to the service of so exalted a lady. I am a labouring man, my name is Sancho Panza, I am married, I have children, and I'm serving as a squire. If in any one of these capacities I can serve your highness, I won't be longer in obeying than your grace is in commanding."

"It's easy to see, Sancho," replied the duchess, "that you've learned to be polite in the school of politeness itself; I mean to say it's easy to see that you have been nursed in the bosom of Señor Don Quixote, who is, of course, the cream of good breeding and flower of ceremony — or cirimony, as you'd say yourself. Fair be the fortunes of such a master and such a servant — the one the polestar of knight-errantry, the other the star of squirely fidelity! Rise, Sancho my friend; I'll repay your courtesy by seeing to it that my lord the duke makes good on the promised gift of the government as soon as possible."

With this the conversation came to an end, and Don Quixote went off to take his midday nap; but the duchess begged Sancho, unless he had a strong desire to sleep, to come and spend the afternoon with her and her damsels in a very cool chamber. Sancho replied that, though he certainly had the habit of sleeping four or five hours in the heat of the day in summer, to serve her excellency he would try with all his might not to sleep even one that day, and that he would come in obedience to her command. And with that he went off. The duke gave fresh orders for treating Don Quixote as a knight-errant, without departing even in the smallest particular from the style in which, as the stories tell us, they used to treat the knights of old.

title: Part 2, Chapter 33
paragraphs: About the delightful discourse the duchess and her damsels had with Sancho Panza, well worth reading and noting

The history records that Sancho did not sleep that afternoon but, in order to keep his word, came to visit the duchess before he had quite finished dinner. She, finding enjoyment in listening to him, made him sit down beside her on a low seat, although Sancho, out of pure good breeding, didn't want to sit down; the duchess, however, told him he was to sit down as a governor and talk as a squire, since in both respects he was worthy of even the chair of the Cid Ruy Diaz the Campeador. Sancho shrugged his shoulders, obeyed, and sat down, and all the duchess's damsels and duennas gathered around him, waiting in profound silence to hear what he would say. It was the duchess, however, who spoke first, saying:

"Now that we are alone, and there is nobody here to overhear us, I should be glad if the señor governor would relieve me of certain doubts I have, arising out of the history of the great Don Quixote that is now in print. One is: given that worthy Sancho never saw Dulcinea — I mean the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — nor took Don Quixote's letter to her, since it was left in the notebook in the Sierra Morena, how did he dare to invent the answer and all that business about finding her sifting wheat, the whole story being a deception and a lie, and so much to the prejudice of the peerless Dulcinea's good name — a thing not at all becoming the character and fidelity of a good squire?"

At these words Sancho, without uttering one in reply, got up from his chair, and with noiseless steps, his body bent and his finger on his lips, he went all round the room lifting up the wall-hangings. This done, he came back to his seat and said, "Now, señora, that I've seen there's no one but the bystanders listening to us on the sly, I'll answer what you've asked me, and anything else you may ask me, without fear or dread. The first thing I have to say is that for my own part I take my master Don Quixote to be stark mad, though sometimes he says things that to my mind, and to everybody's who listens to him, are so wise and run in such a straight furrow that Satan himself could not have said them better. But for all that, really and truly, it's my firm belief that he is cracked. Well then, since this is clear to me, I can risk making him believe things that have neither head nor tail, like that business of the answer to the letter, and that other business of six or eight days ago which isn't yet in any history — I mean the business of the enchantment of my lady Dulcinea. I made him believe she's enchanted, when there's no more truth in it than over the hills of Úbeda."

The duchess begged him to tell her about the enchantment or deception, so Sancho told the whole story exactly as it had happened, and his hearers were not a little amused by it. Then resuming, the duchess said, "In consequence of what worthy Sancho has told me, a doubt starts up in my mind, and there comes a kind of whisper to my ear that says, 'If Don Quixote is mad, crazy, and cracked, and Sancho Panza his squire knows it, and nevertheless serves and follows him, and goes on trusting to his empty promises, there can be no doubt that he must be still madder and sillier than his master; and that being so, it will be cast in your teeth, señora duchess, if you give the said Sancho an island to govern — because how will he who doesn't know how to govern himself know how to govern others?'"

"By God, señora," said Sancho, "that doubt comes at just the right time. Your grace may say it straight out and speak plainly, or however you like, because I know what you say is true; if I were wise, I'd have left my master long ago. But this was my fate, this was my bad luck; I can't help it, I have to follow him. We're from the same village, I've eaten his bread, I'm fond of him, I'm grateful, he gave me his ass-colts, and above all I'm faithful; so it's quite impossible for anything to separate us except the pickaxe and shovel. And if your highness doesn't care to give me the government you promised, God made me without it, and maybe your not giving it to me will be all the better for my conscience — because fool as I am, I know the proverb 'to her hurt the ant got wings,' and it may be that Sancho the squire will get to heaven sooner than Sancho the governor. 'They make as good bread here as in France,' and 'by night all cats are grey,' and 'a hard case enough is his who hasn't broken his fast by two in the afternoon,' and 'there's no stomach a hand's breadth bigger than another,' and the same can be filled 'with straw or hay,' as the saying goes, and 'the little birds of the field have God for their purveyor and caterer,' and 'four yards of Cuenca frieze keep one warmer than four of Segovia broadcloth,' and 'when we quit this world and are put underground the prince travels by as narrow a path as the journeyman,' and 'the Pope's body takes up no more feet of earth than the sacristan's,' for all that the one stands higher than the other; because when we go to our graves we all pack ourselves up and make ourselves small, or rather they pack us up and make us small in spite of ourselves, and then — good night to us. And I say once more: if your ladyship doesn't care to give me the island because I'm a fool, like a wise man I'll take care not to trouble myself about it. I've heard say that 'behind the cross there's the devil,' and that 'all that glitters is not gold,' and that from among the oxen and the ploughs and the yokes, Wamba the husbandman was taken to be made King of Spain, and from among brocades and pleasures and riches, Roderick was taken to be devoured by adders — if the verses of the old ballads don't lie."

"To be sure they don't lie!" exclaimed Doña Rodriguez, the duenna, who was one of the listeners. "There's a ballad that says they put King Rodrigo alive into a tomb full of toads, and adders, and lizards, and that two days afterwards the king, in a plaintive, feeble voice, cried out from inside the tomb—
They gnaw me now, they gnaw me now, There where I most did sin.
And according to that, the gentleman has good reason to say he'd rather be a labouring man than a king, if vermin are going to eat him."

The duchess could not help laughing at the simplicity of her duenna, or wondering at the language and proverbs of Sancho, to whom she said, "Worthy Sancho knows very well that when once a knight has made a promise, he strives to keep it, even if it should cost him his life. My lord and husband the duke, though not one of the errant sort, is none the less a knight for that reason, and will keep his word about the promised island, in spite of the envy and malice of the world. Let Sancho be of good cheer; when he least expects it he'll find himself seated on the throne of his island and seat of dignity, and will take possession of his government — only to discard it for another of three-bordered brocade. The charge I give him is to be careful how he governs his vassals, bearing in mind that they are all loyal and well-born."

"As for governing them well," said Sancho, "there's no need to charge me to do that, because I'm kind-hearted by nature and full of compassion for the poor. 'There's no stealing the loaf from him who kneads and bakes,' and by my faith it won't do to throw false dice with me; I'm an old dog, and I know all about 'tus, tus.' I can be wide awake when need be, and I don't let clouds come before my eyes, because I know where the shoe pinches me. I say so because with me the good will have support and protection, and the bad neither footing nor entry. And it seems to me that in governments, to make a beginning is everything; and perhaps, after being governor for a fortnight, I'll take to the work and know more about it than the field labour I was brought up to."

"You are right, Sancho," said the duchess, "because no one is born ready taught, and bishops are made out of men, not out of stones. But to return to the subject we were discussing just now, the enchantment of the lady Dulcinea: I look upon it as certain, and more than evident, that Sancho's idea of practising a deception on his master — making him believe the peasant girl was Dulcinea and that if he didn't recognise her it must be because she was enchanted — was all the work of one of the enchanters who persecute Don Quixote. Because in truth and earnest, I know from good authority that the coarse country wench who jumped up on the donkey was and is Dulcinea del Toboso, and that worthy Sancho, though he fancies himself the deceiver, is the one who's been deceived; and there's no more reason to doubt the truth of this than of anything else we never saw. Señor Sancho Panza must know that we too have enchanters here who are well disposed to us, and tell us what goes on in the world plainly and distinctly, without subterfuge or deception. And believe me, Sancho, that nimble country lass was and is Dulcinea del Toboso, who is just as enchanted as the mother that bore her; and when we least expect it, we shall see her in her own proper form, and then Sancho will be undeceived of the error he is under now."

"That's all quite possible," said Sancho Panza. "And now I'm willing to believe what my master says about what he saw in the cave of Montesinos, where he says he saw the lady Dulcinea del Toboso in the very same dress and apparel I said I had seen her in when I enchanted her purely to please myself. It must be the other way round, as your ladyship says, because it's impossible to suppose that out of my poor wit such a cunning trick could be cooked up in a moment, nor do I think my master is so mad that by my weak and feeble persuasion he could be made to believe a thing so out of all reason. But, señora, your excellency must not therefore think me ill-disposed, because a dolt like me isn't bound to see into the thoughts and plots of those vile enchanters. I invented all that to escape my master's scolding, not with any intention of hurting him; and if it has turned out differently, there is a God in heaven who judges our hearts."
"That is true," said the duchess. "But tell me, Sancho, what is this you say about the cave of Montesinos? I'd like to know."

Sancho thereupon related to her, word for word, what has already been said about that adventure, and having heard it the duchess said, "From this incident it may be inferred that, since the great Don Quixote says he saw there the same country wench Sancho saw on the way from El Toboso, it is no doubt Dulcinea, and that there are some very active and exceedingly busy enchanters about."

"So I say," said Sancho, "and if my lady Dulcinea is enchanted, so much the worse for her; I'm not going to pick a quarrel with my master's enemies, who seem to be many and spiteful. The truth is that the one I saw was a country wench, and I took her for a country wench; and if that was Dulcinea it must not be laid at my door, nor should I be called to answer for it or take the consequences. But they have to keep nagging at me at every turn — 'Sancho said it, Sancho did it, Sancho here, Sancho there,' as if Sancho was nobody at all, and not that same Sancho Panza who's now going all over the world in books, so Samson Carrasco told me; and he is at least a bachelor of Salamanca, and people of that sort can't lie, except when the whim takes them or they have some very good reason for it. So there's no occasion for anyone to quarrel with me; and besides, I have a good character, and as I've heard my master say, 'a good name is better than great riches.' Just stick me into this government and they'll see wonders, because one who's been a good squire will be a good governor."

"All worthy Sancho's observations," said the duchess, "are Catonian maxims, or at any rate straight out of the very heart of Michael Verino himself, who _florentibus occidit annis_. In fact, to speak in his own style, 'under a bad cloak there's often a good drinker.'"

"Indeed, señora," said Sancho, "I never yet drank out of wickedness; from thirst very likely, because I have nothing of the hypocrite in me. I drink when I'm inclined, or if I'm not inclined, when they offer it to me, so as not to look either strait-laced or ill-bred — because when a friend drinks to your health, what heart can be so hard as not to return it? But if I put on my shoes I don't dirty them. Besides, squires to knights-errant mostly drink water, because they're always wandering among woods, forests and meadows, mountains and crags, without a drop of wine to be had if they gave their eyes for it."
"So I believe," said the duchess. "And now let Sancho go take his sleep, and we'll talk later at greater length, and settle how he may soon go and stick himself into the government, as he says."
Sancho once more kissed the duchess's hand and begged her to let good care be taken of his Dapple, for he was the light of his eyes.
"What is Dapple?" said the duchess.

"My donkey," said Sancho, "which, so as not to call him by that name, I'm accustomed to call Dapple. I begged this lady duenna here to take care of him when I came into the castle, and she got as angry as if I'd called her ugly or old — though it ought to be more natural and proper for duennas to feed donkeys than to ornament chambers. God bless me, what a grudge a gentleman of my village had against these ladies!"
"He must have been some clown," said Doña Rodriguez the duenna; "because if he'd been a gentleman and well-born, he would have exalted them higher than the horns of the moon."

"That'll do," said the duchess; "no more of this. Hush, Doña Rodriguez, and let Señor Panza rest easy and leave the treatment of Dapple to me, because since he is a treasure of Sancho's, I'll set him on the apple of my eye."

"It'll be enough for him to be in the stable," said Sancho, "because neither he nor I are worthy to rest a moment on the apple of your highness's eye, and I'd as soon stab myself as consent to it; for although my master says that in matters of civility it's better to lose by a card too many than a card too few, when it comes to civilities to donkeys we have to watch what we're about and keep within proper bounds."
"Take him to your government, Sancho," said the duchess, "and there you'll be able to make as much of him as you like, and even release him from work and pension him off."
"Don't think, señora duchess, that you've said anything absurd," said Sancho. "I've seen more than two donkeys go to governments, so for me to take mine with me would be nothing new."

Sancho's words made the duchess laugh again and gave her fresh amusement, and dismissing him to sleep she went off to tell the duke the conversation she'd had with him. Between them they plotted and arranged to play a joke on Don Quixote that was to be a rare one and entirely in knight-errantry style, and in that same style they pulled off several more on him, so much in keeping and so cleverly done that they form the best adventures this great history contains.

title: Part 2, Chapter 34
paragraphs: Which relates how they learned the method by which the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso was to be disenchanted — one of the most remarkable adventures in this book

The duke and duchess took enormous delight in the conversation of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, and, more determined than ever to carry out their scheme of playing tricks on the pair that would carry the look and feel of real adventures, they took as their starting point what Don Quixote had already told them about the cave of Montesinos, planning to stage a famous prank on that basis. What astonished the duchess above everything else, though, was that Sancho could be simple enough to accept as gospel truth that Dulcinea had been enchanted, when he himself had been the enchanter and the trickster behind the whole affair. So, having briefed their servants on everything they were to do, six days later they took Don Quixote out hunting, with a retinue of huntsmen and beaters worthy of a crowned king.

They offered Don Quixote a hunting outfit, and Sancho another of the finest green cloth; but Don Quixote refused to put his on, saying that he would soon have to return to the harsh calling of arms and could not travel with wardrobes or baggage. Sancho, on the other hand, accepted what they gave him, intending to sell it at the first chance he got.

When the appointed day came, Don Quixote put on his armor and Sancho dressed himself up, and mounted on his Dapple — for he refused to give the donkey up even though they offered him a horse — he took his place among the crowd of huntsmen. The duchess rode out magnificently dressed, and Don Quixote, out of pure courtesy and good manners, held the rein of her palfrey, although the duke tried to prevent it; and at last they reached a wood lying between two high mountains, where, after taking up various stations, ambush points, and paths, and posting the party in different positions, the hunt opened with a great racket of shouting and hallooing, so that between the baying of the hounds and the blare of the horns nobody could hear anyone else. The duchess dismounted and, with a sharp boar-spear in her hand, stationed herself at a spot where she knew the wild boars usually passed. The duke and Don Quixote dismounted as well and placed themselves on either side of her. Sancho posted himself behind everyone without getting off Dapple, whom he did not dare abandon for fear some harm might come to him. They had hardly formed their line with a number of their servants when they saw a huge boar bearing down on them, hard pressed by the hounds and pursued by the huntsmen, gnashing his teeth and tusks and flinging foam from his mouth. The moment Don Quixote saw him, he braced his shield on his arm, drew his sword, and stepped forward to meet him; the duke did the same with his boar-spear; and the duchess would have gone out in front of them all if the duke had not stopped her. Only Sancho, deserting Dapple at the sight of the formidable beast, ran for it as fast as his legs would carry him and tried in vain to climb a tall oak. While he was clinging to a branch halfway up, struggling toward the top, the bough — such was his bad luck and hard fate — snapped, and as he fell he was caught on a broken stub of the oak and left hanging in midair, unable to reach the ground. Finding himself in this fix, noticing that the green coat was beginning to tear, and reflecting that if the savage animal came that way it might be able to reach him, he began to let out such yells and to cry for help so desperately that everyone who heard him without seeing him was convinced he must be in the jaws of some wild beast. In the end the tusked boar went down, run through by the blades of the many spears leveled against him; and Don Quixote, turning at the sound of Sancho's cries — for he recognized them at once as his — saw him dangling head downward from the oak, with Dapple, who had not abandoned him in his trouble, standing close by; and Cide Hamete remarks that he rarely saw Sancho Panza without seeing Dapple, or Dapple without seeing Sancho Panza, so deep was the attachment and loyalty between the two. Don Quixote went over and unhooked Sancho, who, the moment he found himself on solid ground, examined the tear in his hunting coat and was grieved to the bottom of his heart, for he had thought of that suit as a family estate.

Meanwhile the others had slung the mighty boar across a mule's back, covered it with sprigs of rosemary and branches of myrtle, and carried it off as a trophy of victory to some large field tents that had been pitched in the middle of the wood, where they found the tables set and dinner laid out in a style so grand and lavish that it was easy to gauge the rank and wealth of their hosts. Sancho, showing the duchess the rips in his torn suit, remarked, “If we had been hunting hares, or going after little birds, my coat would have been spared the state it's in now; I don't see what pleasure there can be in lying in wait for an animal that can take your life with a tusk if it reaches you. I remember hearing an old ballad sung that goes,

May you be eaten by bears, as once
Was the famous Favila.”
“That,” said Don Quixote, “was a Gothic king who went out hunting and was devoured by a bear.”

“Exactly,” said Sancho; “and I wouldn't want kings and princes putting themselves in dangers like that for the sake of a pleasure which, to my way of thinking, shouldn't be one at all, since it amounts to killing an animal that has done no harm whatsoever.”

“On the contrary, Sancho, there you are mistaken,” said the duke; “for hunting is more fitting and more necessary for kings and princes than for anyone else. The chase is an image of war: it has its stratagems, its tricks, and its cunning devices for defeating the enemy without risk; in it one must endure bitter cold and unbearable heat; idleness and sleep are held in contempt; the body's strength is built up and the limbs of whoever practices it are made agile; in short, it is a pursuit that can be followed without injuring anyone and with enjoyment for many; and the best part of it is that it is not open to everybody, as other kinds of field sport are — except hawking, which is likewise reserved for kings and great lords. So change your opinion, Sancho, and when you are a governor take up hunting, and you will find it does you good.”

“Not a chance,” said Sancho; “a good governor should be like a man with a broken leg — stay at home;” it would be a fine thing if people went to the trouble of coming to see him on business only to find the governor off in the forest amusing himself; the government would go to ruin that way. Honestly, señor, hunting and entertainments are better suited to idlers than to governors; what I plan to amuse myself with is a game of all fours at Eastertime, and bowls on Sundays and holidays; all this hunting doesn't fit my station or sit well with my conscience.”
“God grant it works out that way,” said the duke, “because there's a long stretch between saying and doing.”

“Be that as it may,” said Sancho, “‘a good payer isn't troubled by pledges,’ and ‘the man God helps does better than the man who rises early,’ and ‘it's the belly that carries the feet, not the feet the belly;’ what I mean is that if God gives me his help and I do my duty honestly, I'll certainly govern better than a gerfalcon. Just let them put a finger in my mouth, and they'll find out whether I can bite or not.”

“The curse of God and all his saints on you, wretched Sancho!” exclaimed Don Quixote. “When will the day come — as I have told you so many times — when I hear you produce a single coherent, sensible remark without proverbs? Your highnesses, I beg you, leave this fool alone, for he will grind your souls between not two but two thousand proverbs, hauled in as timely and as much to the point as — may God give him good health for it, or me, if I'm willing to listen to them!”

“Sancho Panza's proverbs,” said the duchess, “though more numerous than the Greek Commander's, are not to be valued any less for the pithiness of their maxims. Speaking for myself, I can say they give me more pleasure than others that may be more aptly chosen and brought in at a better moment.”

Talking pleasantly in this fashion they left the tent and went into the wood, and the day passed in visiting some of the stations and hiding places, until night came on — not, however, as clear or as calm as might have been expected for the season, since it was then midsummer, but bringing with it a kind of haze that served the duke and duchess's plot very well. So as night was falling, a little after twilight set in, the whole wood suddenly seemed to blaze up on all four sides, and shortly afterward, here, there, and everywhere, an enormous number of trumpets and other instruments of war were heard, as though several troops of cavalry were riding through the wood. The glare of the fires and the noise of the martial instruments all but blinded the eyes and deafened the ears of those standing there, and indeed of everyone in the wood. Then came repeated lelilies, the war cries the Moors raise when they charge into battle; trumpets and clarions blared, drums pounded, fifes shrilled, so continuously and so fast that no one could have kept his senses amid the confused din of so many instruments. The duke was thunderstruck, the duchess amazed, Don Quixote full of wonder, Sancho Panza shaking — and even those in on the secret were frightened. Fear silenced them all, and a postilion got up as a demon rode past in front of them, blowing, instead of a bugle, a huge hollow horn that gave out a hideous, rasping note.
“Ho there, brother courier!” called the duke. “Who are you? Where are you bound? What troops are these that seem to be passing through the wood?”

To which the courier answered in a harsh, grating voice, “I am the devil; I am looking for Don Quixote of La Mancha; the company coming this way is six troops of enchanters, bringing the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso on a triumphal car; she comes under enchantment, together with the gallant Frenchman Montesinos, to instruct Don Quixote in how she, the said lady, may be freed from her enchantment.”

“If you really were the devil, as you claim and as your appearance suggests,” said the duke, “you would have recognized the said knight, Don Quixote of La Mancha, for he is standing here in front of you.”
“By God and on my conscience,” said the devil, “I never noticed him, for my mind is taken up with so many different matters that I was forgetting the chief business I came about.”

“This demon must be an honest fellow and a good Christian,” said Sancho; “otherwise he wouldn't swear by God and his conscience. I'm convinced now that there must be decent souls even down in hell itself.”

Then, without dismounting, the demon turned to Don Quixote and said, “The unfortunate but valiant knight Montesinos sends me to you, Knight of the Lions — and would that I saw you in their claws — charging me to tell you to wait for him wherever I find you, since he brings with him the lady they call Dulcinea del Toboso, so that he may show you what must be done to free her from her enchantment; and since I came for nothing more, I need stay no longer; may demons of my kind be with you, and good angels with these gentlefolk.” And with that he blew his enormous horn, wheeled around, and rode off without waiting for an answer from anyone.

Fresh astonishment seized them all, but especially Sancho and Don Quixote — Sancho at seeing how, in flat defiance of the truth, everyone insisted that Dulcinea was enchanted; Don Quixote because he still could not be certain whether what had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos was real or not; and while he was sunk in these reflections the duke asked him, “Do you intend to wait, Señor Don Quixote?”
“Why not?” he replied. “Here I will wait, fearless and steadfast, though all hell itself should come to attack me.”
“Well, if I see another devil or hear another horn like that last one, I'll wait here about as readily as I'd wait in Flanders,” said Sancho.

Night had now fully closed in, and many lights began to dart about through the wood, just as the fiery vapors rising from the earth — which look to our eyes like shooting stars — streak across the sky; and at the same time a dreadful noise was heard, like the sound made by the solid wheels of ox-carts, whose harsh, unceasing creaking is said to drive off bears and wolves, if there are any along the route. On top of all this commotion came a further disturbance to swell the uproar, for now it truly seemed as though four skirmishes or battles were being fought at once on all four sides of the wood: in one quarter rumbled the dull thunder of a fearsome cannonade, in another countless muskets were being fired, the shouts of the combatants sounded almost at hand, and farther off the Moorish lelilies rose again and again. In short, the bugles, the horns, the clarions, the trumpets, the drums, the cannon, the musket fire, and above everything the tremendous racket of the carts, together made up a din so confused and so terrifying that Don Quixote had to summon all his courage to face it; but Sancho's failed him altogether, and he collapsed in a faint onto the skirt of the duchess's gown. She let him lie there and promptly ordered water to be thrown in his face. This was done, and he had come around by the time one of the creaking-wheeled carts reached the spot. It was drawn by four plodding oxen all draped in black coverings; to each horn was fastened a large lighted wax taper, and on top of the cart was built a raised seat on which sat a venerable old man with a beard whiter than snow itself, and so long that it hung below his waist; he wore a long robe of black buckram, and since the cart bristled with a multitude of candles, everything on it could be seen plainly. Leading it were two hideous demons, likewise dressed in buckram, with faces so frightful that Sancho, having looked at them once, shut his eyes so as not to see them again. When the cart drew level with the spot, the old man rose from his lofty seat, stood, and declared in a loud voice, “I am the sage Lirgandeo,” and without another word the cart rolled on. Behind it came another of the same design, carrying another aged man enthroned, who halted the cart and announced in a voice no less solemn than the first's, “I am the sage Alquife, great friend of Urganda the Unknown,” and passed on. Then a third cart came by at the same pace, but the figure on the throne was not old like the others; he was a big, powerfully built man with a menacing face, who as he came up proclaimed in a voice far hoarser and more devilish, “I am the enchanter Archelaus, mortal enemy of Amadis of Gaul and all his kin,” and then passed on. A short distance farther on the three carts halted and the grinding noise of their wheels stopped, and soon afterward they heard something else — not noise this time, but the sound of sweet, harmonious music, which delighted Sancho, who took it for a good omen; and he said to the duchess, from whose side he would not stir a step or for a single instant, “Señora, where there's music there can't be any mischief.”

“Nor where there are lights and brightness,” said the duchess; to which Sancho answered, “Fire gives light, and it's bright around bonfires, as we can see from the ones surrounding us right now — which may well burn us yet; but music is a sign of feasting and merrymaking.”
“That remains to be seen,” said Don Quixote, who had been listening to all of it; and he was right, as the following chapter shows.

title: Part 2, Chapter 35
paragraphs: In which the instruction given to Don Quixote about the disenchantment of Dulcinea continues, along with other marvellous incidents

Toward them, to the sound of this agreeable music, came what is called a triumphal car, drawn by six grey mules draped in white linen, and on each mule rode a penitent, also robed in white, carrying a large lighted wax taper in his hand. The car was twice — perhaps three times — the size of the earlier ones, and along its front and sides stood twelve more penitents, all white as snow and all holding lighted tapers: a sight to stir fear as much as wonder. On a raised throne sat a nymph wrapped in a multitude of veils of silver tissue, glittering all over with countless embroidered gold spangles, which made her look, if not richly dressed, at least dazzlingly so. Her face was covered with a thin, transparent silk whose weave did not stop anyone from making out the lovely features of a young woman beneath it, and the many lights made it possible to judge both her beauty and her age, which seemed no less than seventeen and not yet twenty. Beside her sat a figure dressed in what they call a robe of state, reaching to the feet, its head covered with a black veil. But the moment the car drew level with the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote, the music of the clarions stopped, and then the lutes and harps on the car fell silent too; the robed figure rose, flung the garment open, lifted the veil from its face, and revealed plainly the shape of Death itself, fleshless and hideous. At the sight Don Quixote grew uneasy, Sancho was frightened, and even the duke and duchess showed a flicker of alarm. Once on its feet, this living Death began to speak, in a drowsy voice and with a tongue that seemed barely awake:

I am that Merlin of whom the legends tell
that the devil was my father — a lie
that time has only made more believable.
Prince of magic, monarch and treasurer
of the lore of Zoroaster, I watch with a jealous eye
as the present age tries to bury
the gallant deeds of bold knights-errant,
who are, and always have been, dear to my heart.
Enchanters, magicians, and their kind
are mostly hard of heart; I am not.
Mine is a tender heart, soft and compassionate,
and its delight is to do good to everyone.
In the dim caverns of gloomy Dis,
where my soul now dwells, tracing
mystic lines and characters, there reached me
the sorrow-laden cry of the fair one,
the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso.
I knew of her enchantment and her fate,
transformed from high-born lady to peasant girl;
and, moved to pity, I first searched the pages
of countless volumes of my devilish art,
and then, sealing my spirit inside
this grim and ghastly skeleton, I have come here
to reveal where the proper remedy lies
to bring relief in so pitiful a case.
O you, glory and pride of all who wear
the adamantine steel! O shining light,
O beacon, polestar, path, and guide of all
who scorn sleep and the lazy featherbed
to take up the toilsome life of blood-stained arms!
To you, great hero beyond all praise,
La Mancha's splendor and Iberia's star,
Don Quixote, as wise as you are brave — to you I say:
for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso
to recover her original form and beauty,
your squire Sancho must lay
three thousand three hundred lashes
on his own sturdy buttocks, bared to the heavens,
and they must smart and sting and hurt him well.
So those who authored her misfortune have decreed,
and that, ladies and gentlemen, is why I have come.

“By everything that's holy,” Sancho burst out at this, “I'd just as soon give myself three stabs with a dagger as three lashes, never mind three thousand. The devil can take this method of disenchanting! I don't see what my backside has to do with enchantments. By God, if Señor Merlin hasn't found some other way of disenchanting the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, she can go to her grave enchanted.”

“And I'll take you, Don Clown stuffed with garlic,” said Don Quixote, “and tie you to a tree as naked as the day your mother bore you, and give you not three thousand three hundred lashes but six thousand six hundred, laid on so firmly that they won't come off even if you try three thousand three hundred times. And don't answer me a single word, or I'll rip the soul out of you.”

Hearing this, Merlin said, “That will not do, for the lashes the worthy Sancho must receive have to be given of his own free will, not by force, and at whatever time he chooses — no deadline has been set for him. He is also permitted, if he wants to cut the pain of this whipping in half, to have the lashes delivered by another's hand, even if that hand is a somewhat heavy one.”

“No hand shall touch me — not my own, not anyone else's, heavy or weighable,” said Sancho. “Did I give birth to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, that my backside should pay for the sins of her eyes? It's my master who's a part of her — he's forever calling her 'my life' and 'my soul,' his stay and his prop — so he may and should whip himself for her sake and go to all the trouble her disenchantment requires. But me, whip myself? Abernuncio!”

The moment Sancho finished speaking, the silver-clad nymph beside Merlin's ghost rose to her feet, and lifting the thin veil from her face she revealed one that struck everybody as something more than exceedingly beautiful; and with a masculine boldness, in a voice not particularly ladylike, she addressed Sancho directly: “You wretched squire, soul of a water-jug, heart of cork, with bowels of flint and gravel — if they ordered you, you brazen thief, to throw yourself down from some high tower; if they asked you, enemy of the human race, to swallow a dozen toads, two dozen lizards, and three dozen adders; if they wanted you to butcher your wife and children with a sharp and murderous scimitar, nobody would be surprised at your turning stubborn and squeamish. But to make such a fuss over three thousand three hundred lashes — which every poor little charity-boy gets in a month — is enough to amaze, astonish, and stupefy the compassionate hearts of all who hear of it, and of all who will ever come to hear of it in times to come. Turn, you miserable, hard-hearted animal — turn, I say, those skittish owl's eyes of yours on these eyes of mine, which have been compared to radiant stars, and you will see them weeping in trickles and streams, cutting furrows, tracks, and pathways across the fair fields of my cheeks. Let it move you, you cunning, ill-natured monster, that my blooming youth — still in its teens, for I am not yet twenty — is wasting and withering away beneath the husk of a coarse peasant girl; and if I do not appear in that shape right now, it is a special favour Señor Merlin here has granted me, for the sole purpose that my beauty might soften you; for the tears of beauty in distress turn rocks to cotton and tigers to ewes. Lay on to that hide of yours, you great unbroken brute; rouse that lusty energy of yours, which only ever drives you to eat and eat again, and set free the smoothness of my flesh, the gentleness of my nature, and the loveliness of my face. And if you will not relent or see reason for my sake, do it for the sake of that poor knight beside you — your master, I mean — whose soul I can see at this very moment lodged in his throat, not ten fingers' breadth from his lips, waiting only for your harsh or yielding answer either to escape through his mouth or to sink back down into his stomach.”
On hearing this, Don Quixote felt his throat and, turning to the duke, said, “By God, señor, Dulcinea is telling the truth — here is my soul, stuck in my throat like the nut of a crossbow.”
“And what do you say to that, Sancho?” asked the duchess.
“I say, señora,” Sancho answered, “exactly what I said before: as far as the lashes go — abernuncio!”
“Abrenuncio is what you should say, Sancho, not the way you put it,” said the duke.

“Leave me alone, your highness,” said Sancho. “I'm in no mood just now to be fussing over fine points or a letter more or less, because these lashes that are to be given me — or that I'm to give myself — have rattled me so badly I don't know what I'm saying or doing. But what I'd like to know from this lady, my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, is where she learned this way she has of asking for favours. She comes asking me to flay my own flesh with a whip, and she calls me soul of a water-jug and great unbroken brute and a whole string of foul names the devil is welcome to. Is my flesh made of brass? Is it any business of mine whether she's enchanted or not? Does she bring along a basket of fine linen — shirts, kerchiefs, socks (not that I wear any) — to win me over? No, nothing but one insult after another, even though she knows the proverb they use around here, that 'an ass loaded with gold climbs a mountain lightly,' and 'gifts break rocks,' and 'pray to God and keep swinging the hammer,' and 'one “take this” is worth more than two “I'll-give-you's.”' Then there's my master, who ought to be stroking me down and petting me until I turn soft as wool and carded cotton — instead he says that if he gets his hands on me, he'll tie me naked to a tree and double the count of lashes on me. These tender-hearted gentlefolk ought to remember that it's not just a squire they're asking to whip himself, but a governor — as if it were as easy as 'have a drink with your cherries.' Let them learn — plague take them — the proper way to ask, to plead, and to behave; all times are not alike, and people aren't always in a good humour. Right now I'm fit to burst with grief at seeing my green coat torn, and here they come asking me to whip myself of my own free will, when I've as little appetite for it as for turning cacique.”

“Well then, friend Sancho, the plain fact is,” said the duke, “that unless you turn softer than a ripe fig, you will never lay hands on the governorship. A fine thing it would be for me to send my islanders a cruel governor with flinty insides, one who won't bend to the tears of damsels in distress or to the entreaties of wise, commanding, venerable enchanters and sages. In short, Sancho: either you whip yourself, or someone else whips you, or you don't become governor.”
“Señor,” said Sancho, “couldn't I be given two days' grace to think over what's best for me?”

“No, certainly not,” said Merlin. “Here, this minute, on this very spot, the matter must be settled: either Dulcinea goes back to the cave of Montesinos and her former condition as a peasant girl, or in her present form she will be carried off to the Elysian Fields, where she will wait until the full tally of lashes is complete.”

“Come now, Sancho!” said the duchess. “Show some courage, and some gratitude for your master Don Quixote's bread, which you have eaten; we are all bound to serve and please him for his benevolent nature and his lofty deeds of chivalry. Say yes to this whipping, my son; send the devil packing back to the devil, and leave fear to the faint-hearted, for 'a stout heart breaks bad luck,' as you know perfectly well.”

To this Sancho replied with a remark that had nothing to do with the matter at hand; addressing Merlin, he said, “Will your worship tell me one thing, Señor Merlin? When that courier devil rode up, he gave my master a message from Señor Montesinos, telling him to wait for him here, because he was coming to arrange how the lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso was to be disenchanted — but up to now we've seen no Montesinos, nor anything like him.”

To which Merlin answered, “The devil, Sancho, is an ignoramus and a thorough scoundrel. I sent him to find your master with a message from me, not from Montesinos — for Montesinos is in his cave expecting, or more accurately awaiting, his own disenchantment, since there's still the tail of that business left to skin. If he owes you anything, or you have any dealings to settle with him, I'll fetch him and set him down wherever you choose. For the present, make up your mind to accept this penance; believe me, it will do you a great deal of good, for soul as well as body — for your soul, because of the charity with which you'll perform it; for your body, because I know you're of a full-blooded constitution, and drawing off a little blood will do you no harm.”

“The world is full of doctors — even the enchanters turn out to be doctors,” said Sancho. “Still, since everyone keeps telling me the same thing — though I can't see it myself — I declare I'm willing to give myself the three thousand three hundred lashes, on condition that I lay them on whenever I please, with no days or dates fixed; and I'll try to get out of the debt as fast as I can, so the world can enjoy the beauty of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso — since it appears, contrary to what I'd thought, that she really is beautiful after all. There must be another condition too: I'm not to be obliged to draw blood with the scourge, and if some of the lashes turn out no harder than fly-swatters, they still count. Item: if I should lose track of the tally, Señor Merlin, who knows everything, is to keep count and let me know how many are still owing or over the number.”

“There will be no need to notify you of any extras,” said Merlin, “because the moment you reach the full number, the lady Dulcinea will be disenchanted then and there, on the very instant, and in her gratitude she will come looking for the worthy Sancho to thank him — and even reward him — for the good deed. So you have no reason to fret about lashes too many or too few; heaven forbid I should cheat anyone out of so much as a hair of his head.”
“Well then, into God's hands with it,” said Sancho. “In this hard spot I find myself in, I give in; I say I accept the penance, on the conditions laid down.”

The instant Sancho spoke these last words, the music of the clarions struck up again and another volley of muskets went off, and Don Quixote threw himself on Sancho's neck, kissing him over and over on the forehead and cheeks. The duke and duchess showed the liveliest satisfaction, the car began to roll on, and as it passed, the fair Dulcinea bowed her head to the duke and duchess and dropped a deep curtsey to Sancho.

And now bright, smiling dawn came hurrying on; the flowers of the field lifted their refreshed heads, and the crystal waters of the brooks, murmuring over the grey and white pebbles, ran to pay their tribute to the rivers that awaited them. The glad earth, the cloudless sky, the fresh breeze, the clear light — each and all gave promise that the day now treading on the skirts of morning would be calm and bright. The duke and duchess, delighted with their hunt and with how cleverly and successfully they had carried out their scheme, returned to their castle resolved to push the joke further; for to them no reality could offer more amusement.

title: Part 2, Chapter 36
